headings.text: 🧬 The families, and which patterns belong to each

notes.html:
Thirteen pointer notes, grouped by the family each pattern belongs to. The family tells you what kind of problem it solves; the catalogue explains each pattern once; the item notes add only the LLD-round layer. Read each arrow as a sentence: the pattern selector chooses from the behavioural family.

Green = holds 🔴 CORE items, blue = 🟡 SUPPORTING and 🟢 BREADTH items, grey = outside this folder.

Reading order:14 strategy18 state15 factory17 observer26 pattern overuse16 singleton19 command20 decorator21 builder23 chain of responsibility25 repository22 template method24 adapter and facade

The families, and which patterns belong to each

Family The question it answers Items in this folder Also in the catalogue (no item note) Catalogue file
Creational how does an object get made, and who decides which one? 15 factory & abstract factory · 16 singleton · 21 builder prototype, object pool, dependency injection creational
Structural how are objects wrapped or composed into something larger? 20 decorator · 24 adapter & facade proxy, composite, flyweight, bridge structural
🎭 Behavioural how does behaviour vary, and how do objects talk? 14 strategy · 17 observer · 18 state · 19 command · 22 template method · 23 chain of responsibility iterator, mediator, memento, visitor, interpreter, null object behavioral
🗄️ Persistence seam how does storage stay out of the domain? 25 repository & unit of work — not a GoF pattern; it comes from enterprise application architecture
Judgment should there be a pattern here at all? 26 pattern overuse the ten anti-patterns anti-patterns

Owners

Idea Owner note
What each pattern is: structure, participants, JDK examples the catalogue file for its family
Which pattern, starting from a requirement sentence pattern selector
Which pattern, starting from a code smell catalogue decision tree
Real production problems and the stack of patterns that ships industry problem playbook
For each pattern: when to reach for it in a round, the follow-up it absorbs, the sentence to say its item note, 14–25
The budget of three or four extension points per round 26

Polymorphism, which every behavioural pattern is built on OOP: four pillars, not these notes
Why double-checked locking needs volatile the Java concurrency notes, linked from 16

Which family?

This tree only narrows to a family. Choosing the pattern inside it is the pattern selector's job.

  • ✋ No pattern (26): if the requirement names a plural or the interviewer asks "now add X", come back in.
  • Creational: if the object is simple and there is one kind, a constructor is enough.
  • Structural: if you own the class and can change it, change it; wrappers are for what you can't or shouldn't edit.
  • 🎭 Behavioural: if the behaviour depends on a lifecycle stage, it is state; if it is a policy chosen from outside, it is strategy.

At a glance

Item Pattern Family Reach for it when the requirement says…
14 strategy 🔴 behavioural "make it configurable": pricing, scheduling, matching
15 factory, abstract factory 🔴 creational create by a type code; replace a switch on an enum
16 singleton 🔴 creational exactly one instance, and you can defend its testability
17 observer 🔴 behavioural "notify", "broadcast", "display updates"
18 state 🔴 behavioural a lifecycle: created → held → confirmed → expired
19 command 🟡 behavioural undo, a request queue, scheduled jobs
20 decorator 🟡 structural add-ons priced on top of a base
21 builder 🟡 creational many optional fields; an immutable result
22 template method 🟢 behavioural fixed steps with one or two that differ
23 chain of responsibility 🟡 behavioural middleware, approvals, validation pipelines
24 adapter, facade 🟢 structural a third-party boundary; several providers
25 repository, unit of work 🟡 persistence seam storage kept out of the domain
26 pattern overuse 🔴 judgment always: name a pattern only when it removes a future edit

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: a pattern is a named way of making one future change cheap. Strategy and state between them cover most problems in Part B.
  • The two most-confused pairs: strategy vs state (chosen from outside vs changes itself as the lifecycle moves) · the four wrappers: adapter, facade, decorator, proxy (disambiguated in structural).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the families table, the at-a-glance table, and the pattern selector's lookup.
  • Cross-section links: the reasons for a seam are in §0 foundations and §2; thread-safety of singleton and observer is in §4. Content gaps: no item note for proxy or composite, the two catalogue patterns most likely to come up after these.

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Strategy — intent, structure, applicability — Strategy Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks
  • Strategy — the diagram-and-trade-offs version — Strategy (refactoring.guru)
  • The refactoring that produces it — Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (refactoring.com)
  • The JDK's own strategy interface — Comparator (Java SE 17)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/behavioral.md. This note is the LLD-round layer with runnable code. Where it sits among the other patterns: chapter map.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What varies, in one phrase? A policy: pricing, scheduling, matching, eviction, splitting, allocation.
The follow-up it absorbs? "Now add surge / weekend / nearest-car": a new class, zero edits.
One strategy vs a list of rules? A list when rules stack (coupon + weekend + tax); a single one when exactly one applies.
Strategy vs State? Strategy: the caller picks the algorithm. State: the object swaps it itself on transitions.
When is it overkill? One implementation and no named future requirement; or a closed set, where an enum with behaviour does it.
Draw by hand: the class diagram PricingEngine holds a list of PricingRule; WeekendSurcharge, FlatCoupon and a lambda implement it.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Strategy puts one policy behind an interface so the class using it doesn't know which algorithm runs. In a ticket system, pricing goes behind PricingRule; the engine folds the price through a list of rules. When the interviewer says "add weekend pricing," I write one new class and register it — the engine doesn't change. That's the whole LLD rubric in one move. The nuance is ordering: when rules stack, the order is part of the contract, and I make it explicit rather than accidental.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What's the difference between Strategy and just passing a lambda?

Nothing structural. A functional interface with one method is a strategy, and in Java or Python a lambda is the lightest implementation of it. Comparator is the JDK's canonical strategy and most people pass it as a lambda.

Reach for a named class when the strategy carries state or configuration (a coupon table, a surge multiplier from config), needs its own tests, or has a domain name worth reading in a stack trace. Reach for a lambda for one-line, stateless rules. Both coexist in the code below.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Pricing has five rules. One PricingStrategy per combination, or a list of composable rules?

One strategy per combination explodes: weekend × coupon × member × festival is sixteen classes, and every new rule doubles the count. A list of independent rules applied in sequence grows linearly, one class per rule, and the engine is a fold over the list.

The price of composability is that order becomes semantics. A 20% surcharge followed by a flat ₹50 discount gives a different total than the reverse. So the order must be deliberate: configured in one place and covered by a test. If rules genuinely conflict ("best of coupon or member discount, never both"), that is a rule that selects between sub-rules, which is still a PricingRule.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Rules now come from a config service and change at runtime. What breaks?

First, consistency within one quote: if the rule list is swapped halfway through a fold, one price is computed with half the old rules and half the new. Fix it with an immutable snapshot per request: hold the list in an AtomicReference<List<PricingRule>> and read it once at the top of price().

Second, quote-versus-charge drift: the user sees ₹370, the config changes, and payment charges ₹390. The fix is a domain one, not a locking one: the quote records the rule-set version and the charge honours the quoted price for its validity window.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design dynamic surge pricing for a ride-hailing app using this pattern.

Start with the constraint: the surge multiplier depends on live supply and demand per geo-cell, and a price must stay stable for the user for a minute or two. So the strategy can't compute demand itself; it reads a precomputed multiplier.

FareEngine holds a list of FareRules: BaseFare(distance, time), SurgeRule(SurgeSource), PromoRule, TollRule. SurgeSource is itself an interface: an in-memory map in the interview, a cache filled by a stream job in production. The quote is stored with the multiplier it used and an expiry, which is what the charge honours. The failure to watch first is a stale or missing surge value: the rule needs a defined fallback (multiplier 1.0 and an alert), because a surge rule that throws takes pricing down for a whole city.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Strategy State Template Method Enum with behaviour
What varies the algorithm for one policy behaviour per lifecycle stage some steps of a fixed skeleton behaviour per constant
Who chooses the caller or config the object itself, on a transition the subclass, at compile time the constant
Mechanism composition composition inheritance constant-specific bodies
Open to new variants? yes: a new class yes: a new state class yes: a new subclass no: edit the enum
Use when an open-ended set of policies transitions change behaviour one or two steps vary a closed, small, stable set

Reach for it when:

  • the problem statement names a policy that will plausibly change: pricing, fees, scheduling, dispatch, matching, eviction, split rules. These are the axes interviewers pick for the follow-up;
  • you are about to write a switch or if-chain whose branches are whole algorithms (FCFS vs SCAN vs LOOK elevator dispatch), not one-line differences;
  • the variants need independent tests, or the choice is made at runtime from config, user tier or city.

DEPTH BLOCK

5. How the Mechanism Works

Three roles, and the arrows only ever point at the interface.

  • Strategy interface (PricingRule): one method, named after the policy, taking everything a rule may need in a context object so new rules don't force a signature change.
  • Concrete strategies (WeekendSurcharge, FlatCoupon): each owns exactly one rule and is testable alone.
  • Context (PricingEngine): receives its strategies through the constructor (item 13) and never branches on which ones it has.

The maths is a left fold: price = rₙ(…r₂(r₁(base))). Function composition is not commutative, so the list order is part of the pricing contract.

Why this matters in practice: policies change on a marketing calendar, not an engineering one. A festival discount goes live on Friday and is gone on Monday. Behind Strategy, that campaign is a new class plus a config entry, and removing it is deleting a line; inside an if chain it is an edit to the most critical code path, twice.

6. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — ticket pricing with a composable rule list. Compiled and run (java -ea).

// File: StrategyDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

// Base fare lives on the enum: a closed set, so no strategy needed here (-> item 35).
enum SeatClass {
    SILVER("200.00"), GOLD("350.00"), RECLINER("600.00");
    final BigDecimal baseFare;
    SeatClass(String fare) { this.baseFare = new BigDecimal(fare); }
}

// Everything a rule may need, in one object: new rules never change the signature.
record PriceContext(SeatClass seatClass, LocalDate showDate, String couponCode) {}

// The strategy interface. Functional, so a lambda is a valid implementation.
@FunctionalInterface
interface PricingRule {
    BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal current, PriceContext ctx);
}

final class WeekendSurcharge implements PricingRule {
    private static final BigDecimal MULTIPLIER = new BigDecimal("1.20");

    @Override
    public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal current, PriceContext ctx) {
        DayOfWeek day = ctx.showDate().getDayOfWeek();
        boolean weekend = day == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY || day == DayOfWeek.SUNDAY;
        return weekend ? current.multiply(MULTIPLIER) : current;
    }
}

final class FlatCoupon implements PricingRule {
    private final Map<String, BigDecimal> discounts;   // injected: rule carries config

    FlatCoupon(Map<String, BigDecimal> discounts) { this.discounts = Map.copyOf(discounts); }

    @Override
    public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal current, PriceContext ctx) {
        if (ctx.couponCode() == null) return current;
        BigDecimal off = discounts.getOrDefault(ctx.couponCode(), BigDecimal.ZERO);
        return current.subtract(off).max(BigDecimal.ZERO);   // never below zero
    }
}

// The context. It never asks which rules it holds.
final class PricingEngine {
    private final List<PricingRule> rules;   // ORDER IS SEMANTICS: surcharge before discount

    PricingEngine(List<PricingRule> rules) { this.rules = List.copyOf(rules); }

    BigDecimal price(PriceContext ctx) {
        BigDecimal price = ctx.seatClass().baseFare;
        for (PricingRule rule : rules) {
            price = rule.apply(price, ctx);
        }
        return price.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);   // money: BigDecimal, fixed scale (-> item 37)
    }
}

public class StrategyDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PricingRule weekend = new WeekendSurcharge();
        PricingRule coupon = new FlatCoupon(Map.of("FLAT50", new BigDecimal("50.00")));
        PricingEngine engine = new PricingEngine(List.of(weekend, coupon));

        PriceContext saturday = new PriceContext(SeatClass.GOLD, LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 19), "FLAT50");
        PriceContext wednesday = new PriceContext(SeatClass.GOLD, LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 16), null);

        System.out.println("GOLD, Sat, FLAT50 = " + engine.price(saturday));
        System.out.println("GOLD, Wed, none   = " + engine.price(wednesday));

        // Follow-up "add 18% GST": a new rule, zero edits to PricingEngine or existing rules.
        PricingRule gst = (current, ctx) -> current.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.18"));
        PricingEngine withTax = new PricingEngine(List.of(weekend, coupon, gst));
        System.out.println("GOLD, Sat, +GST   = " + withTax.price(saturday));

        assert engine.price(saturday).equals(new BigDecimal("370.00"));
        assert withTax.price(saturday).equals(new BigDecimal("436.60"));
    }
}

GOLD, Sat, FLAT50 = 370.00
GOLD, Wed, none   = 350.00
GOLD, Sat, +GST   = 436.60

Python 3.9+ — the same design. In Python a strategy is usually just a callable; a class earns its place only when the rule carries state. It prints the same three lines.

# File: strategy_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import ROUND_HALF_UP, Decimal
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable, Mapping, Optional, Sequence


class SeatClass(Enum):
    SILVER = Decimal("200.00")
    GOLD = Decimal("350.00")
    RECLINER = Decimal("600.00")

    @property
    def base_fare(self) -> Decimal:
        return self.value


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PriceContext:
    seat_class: SeatClass
    show_date: date
    coupon_code: Optional[str] = None


# The strategy "interface" is a type alias for a callable. No ABC needed.
PricingRule = Callable[[Decimal, PriceContext], Decimal]


def weekend_surcharge(current: Decimal, ctx: PriceContext) -> Decimal:
    # Stateless rule -> a plain function.
    is_weekend = ctx.show_date.weekday() >= 5   # 5 = Saturday, 6 = Sunday
    return current * Decimal("1.20") if is_weekend else current


class FlatCoupon:
    """Stateful rule -> a class with __call__, so it still satisfies PricingRule."""

    def __init__(self, discounts: Mapping[str, Decimal]) -> None:
        self._discounts = dict(discounts)

    def __call__(self, current: Decimal, ctx: PriceContext) -> Decimal:
        if ctx.coupon_code is None:
            return current
        off = self._discounts.get(ctx.coupon_code, Decimal("0"))
        return max(current - off, Decimal("0"))


class PricingEngine:
    def __init__(self, rules: Sequence[PricingRule]) -> None:
        self._rules = tuple(rules)   # immutable snapshot; order is part of the contract

    def price(self, ctx: PriceContext) -> Decimal:
        price = ctx.seat_class.base_fare
        for rule in self._rules:
            price = rule(price, ctx)
        return price.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    coupon = FlatCoupon({"FLAT50": Decimal("50.00")})
    engine = PricingEngine([weekend_surcharge, coupon])

    saturday = PriceContext(SeatClass.GOLD, date(2026, 9, 19), "FLAT50")
    wednesday = PriceContext(SeatClass.GOLD, date(2026, 9, 16))

    print("GOLD, Sat, FLAT50 =", engine.price(saturday))
    print("GOLD, Wed, none   =", engine.price(wednesday))

    # Follow-up "add 18% GST": one lambda, zero edits.
    with_tax = PricingEngine([weekend_surcharge, coupon, lambda p, c: p * Decimal("1.18")])
    print("GOLD, Sat, +GST   =", with_tax.price(saturday))

    assert engine.price(saturday) == Decimal("370.00")
    assert with_tax.price(saturday) == Decimal("436.60")

7. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Input: PriceContext(GOLD, 2026-09-19 (a Saturday), "FLAT50"), rules [WeekendSurcharge, FlatCoupon].

Step What runs Price after
1 base fare from SeatClass.GOLD 350.00
2 WeekendSurcharge: Saturday, so × 1.20 420.00
3 FlatCoupon: "FLAT50" found, so − 50.00 370.00
4 setScale(2, HALF_UP), once, at the end 370.00
5 with a third rule, GST: × 1.18 436.60
  1. Base fare comes from the enum, not from a rule. Seat classes are a closed set, so an enum carrying its fare is lighter than a BaseFareStrategy.
  2. The surcharge sees 350.00 because it is first in the list. Had the coupon run first, the result would be (350 − 50) × 1.20 = 360.00: a ₹10 difference that is a business decision, not a bug.
  3. The coupon clamps at zero, so a large coupon on a cheap seat can't produce a negative charge.
  4. Scaling happens once, at the end. Rounding inside each rule would compound rounding error across the fold.
  5. The GST follow-up added a lambda. PricingEngine, WeekendSurcharge and FlatCoupon were not opened. That is the scoring event.

8. Where You Already Use It

  • JDK: Comparator passed to List.sort and TreeMap; RejectedExecutionHandler on ThreadPoolExecutor (abort, caller-runs and discard are interchangeable policies).
  • Spring: PlatformTransactionManager implementations; Spring Security's PasswordEncoder.
  • Python standard library: the key= function on sorted, and the default= hook in json.dumps.

Pitfalls

  • "Strategy removes the switch entirely"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the pattern is taught as the cure for conditionals, and the context class really does end up with none.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: something still decides which rule applies: a factory, a config map, the place where objects are wired together.
    ↳ Think instead: the decision moves to one place. The win is that it exists once, not in every method that prices something.
  • "Strategy needs an interface plus a hierarchy of classes"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that is how the original pattern books draw it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: any single-method function type is a strategy. Comparator lambdas, Python callables and Function<T,R> all qualify.
    ↳ Think instead: Strategy is a role, not a structure. A named class is a choice for rules that carry state or deserve their own tests.
  • Not the same: Strategy vs State
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the class diagrams are identical: a context holding an interface with several implementations.
    ↳ Difference: a strategy is chosen from outside and usually stays put; a state replaces itself as the object moves through its lifecycle, and the states know about each other.
    ↳ Think instead: ask who changes it. The caller or config: Strategy. The object, in response to an event: State.
  • Don't create a strategy with nothing to vary.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: an interface feels like good design, and "program to an interface" sounds like a rule.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a BaseFareStrategy, a TaxStrategy and a RoundingStrategy on a parking lot with one fee rule reads as pattern recitation, and costs reading time (item 26).
    ↳ Do instead: for a closed, small set use an enum with behaviour; when variants differ by a number, use one rule with a parameter.
  • Don't leave rule order implicit.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a list of rules looks like a set, and in the first example the order happens to be right.
    ↳ What goes wrong: surcharge-then-coupon gives ₹370 and coupon-then-surcharge gives ₹360. Interviewers ask "coupon before or after the surcharge?" on purpose.
    ↳ Do instead: define the order in one place, say so out loud, and pin it with a test.
  • Don't name the pattern in place of the future edit.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "I'll use Strategy here" sounds like the expected answer.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it earns little, and it hides whether you know why. The same goes for building the strategy inside the context (new WeekendSurcharge() in PricingEngine): a hard-coded dependency in a pattern costume.
    ↳ Do instead: "pricing will change, so weekend pricing becomes a new class, not an if in price()", and inject the rules (item 7).

Connections

  • The rubric it satisfies — open/closed as the scoring rubric; explained from first principles in SOLID.
  • How strategies reach the context — constructor dependency injection.
  • Choose these instead — enum with behaviour for a closed, small set; template method when one step of a fixed skeleton varies; state when the object changes its own behaviour.
  • Works with — factory, which picks the strategy to build from config; decorator, which can wrap a strategy, for example to log each rule's effect.
  • Money in the signature — never use double for money.
  • Where it is the centrepiece — elevator (SchedulingStrategy) and parking lot (spot allocation and fee models).
  • Deciding it from a requirement — the pattern selector.

notes.title: Factory & Abstract Factory

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Factory Method — Factory method Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Abstract Factory — Abstract Factory Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Factory Method, with structure diagram — Factory Method (refactoring.guru)

  • Bonus — Abstract Factory (refactoring.guru)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/creational.md. This note is the LLD-round layer with runnable code.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Simple factory vs Factory Method? Simple: one method with a switch. Factory Method: a subclass overrides the creation step.
Abstract Factory in one line? Creates a family of related objects that must match each other.
Does a simple factory remove the switch? No — it centralises it in one place. Registry-based factories remove it.
Why an exhaustive switch expression on an enum? No default: adding a constant becomes a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
Static factory method (List.of) = GoF Factory Method? No. Named constructor vs. overridable creation hook — different things.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

A factory moves "which concrete class do I build?" out of business code. The moment I'm about to write switch (type) { case SMS: new SmsChannel() } inside a service, I move it into a factory so the choice exists once. If new types must be added without editing anything, I use a registry — a map from key to constructor. Abstract Factory is different: it builds a matched family, like a payment provider's client and its webhook verifier, so you can't accidentally pair one provider's client with another's verifier. The follow-up it absorbs is "now support a third type."

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through simple factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory — how are they different?

Seen in the wild: this is the comparative question for creational patterns; interviewers ask it almost verbatim.

A simple factory is one method that takes a type code and returns an instance; it contains the switch. It isn't a GoF pattern, but it's the one you'll actually write most. Factory Method is inheritance-based: a base class defines an algorithm that calls an abstract createX(), and each subclass decides what X is. Abstract Factory is an object with several creation methods whose products are designed to work together — swap the factory and the whole family changes consistently.

The discriminating question is what varies: one product by type code (simple factory or registry), one product by subclass (Factory Method), or a consistent set of products (Abstract Factory).

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A simple factory still has a switch. Why is that better than the switch in the service?

Really testing: whether you can be honest about a pattern's limits instead of overselling it.

Because the change cost is different. With the switch in business code, every service that creates channels has its own copy, and adding WHATSAPP is an edit in N places with N chances to miss one. With the simple factory, it's one edit in one file. And if the switch is an exhaustive switch expression over an enum, the compiler finds the missed case for you.

It is not open/closed, and it's worth saying so. When types must be added without touching the factory — a plugin, a partner team, a config-driven channel — use a registry: Map<String, Supplier<Channel>> with register(). The cost is losing compile-time exhaustiveness: an unknown key becomes a runtime error, so validate configured keys at startup.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your SmsChannel needs an API client, a rate limiter and a retry policy. How does the factory build it?

The factory can't new those dependencies itself without becoming a hard-wired god object. Two clean options: the factory is constructed at the composition root with the shared dependencies injected, and passes them to what it builds; or the registry stores Suppliers that capture already-built dependencies in a closure. Either way, the factory decides which class, and the composition root decides with what.

The second question is instance lifecycle. A stateless channel should be built once and reused — creating a new HTTP client per notification exhausts connections under load. Stateful per-request objects are created fresh. Say which one each product is; a DI container is essentially a factory that answers this question with scopes.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Partner teams must add notification channels without redeploying the core service. Design it.

Really testing: whether a registry factory scales up into a plugin architecture with a real failure story.

The highest-stakes constraint is that core code can't know channel names at compile time. So the extension point is a NotificationChannelProvider interface with key() and create(ChannelDeps), discovered at startup — java.util.ServiceLoader in Java, importlib.metadata entry points in Python — and registered into the channel registry.

Composition: loader discovers providers → registry validates uniqueness of keys → routing config maps user preference to a key → the registry creates the channel. Channels are wrapped by a retry/metrics decorator at registration so partner code gets consistent observability for free (→ item 20).

The failure to monitor first is a configured key with no registered provider. Fail at startup rather than on the first notification, and emit a per-key "created / failed" counter so a missing plugin shows up as a flatline, not as silent dropped messages.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Simple factory Registry factory Factory Method Abstract Factory
What varies One product by type code One product by key One product by subclass A family of products
Mechanism switch in one method Map<key, Supplier> Abstract create() overridden Interface with several create methods
Add a variant Edit the factory register() — no edit New subclass New factory class
Compile-time safety exhaustive switch unknown key at runtime
LLD use Vehicle/spot by enum Plugins, config-driven Framework hooks Provider kits, UI themes

DEPTH BLOCK

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

The invariant all four forms share: concrete class names appear in exactly one place. Business code depends on NotificationChannel and PaymentProviderKit, never on SmsChannel or AcmePayClient.

  • Simple factory — a pure function type → instance. Its value is centralisation plus compiler-checked exhaustiveness.

  • Registry — the switch becomes data. Lookup is O(1); the set of types is open at runtime.

  • Factory Method — the base class owns the workflow and defers one creation step to subclasses.

  • Abstract Factory — one object guarantees that products from the same family are used together.

6. Why It Matters in Production

Object creation is where configuration meets code: which payment provider this merchant uses, which channel this user prefers, which storage backend this region has. Without a factory, that knowledge leaks into every service as if (provider == ...) blocks, and adding a provider becomes a search-and-edit across the codebase. With a factory — and especially an abstract factory for provider integrations — onboarding a new provider is one new class and one registration, and a mismatched pair (provider A's client verifying provider B's webhooks) is structurally impossible rather than a production incident.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — notification channels (simple factory, registry, Factory Method) and a payment provider kit (Abstract Factory). AcmePay and ZetaPay are fictional providers.

// File: FactoryDemo.java
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

// ---------- Products ----------
interface NotificationChannel {
    String send(String userId, String message);
}

final class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel {
    public String send(String userId, String message) { return "EMAIL to " + userId + ": " + message; }
}

final class SmsChannel implements NotificationChannel {
    public String send(String userId, String message) { return "SMS to " + userId + ": " + message; }
}

enum ChannelType { EMAIL, SMS }

// ---------- 1. Simple factory: the switch exists, but exactly once ----------
final class SimpleChannelFactory {
    private SimpleChannelFactory() {}

    static NotificationChannel create(ChannelType type) {
        // Switch EXPRESSION with no default: add PUSH to the enum and this stops compiling.
        return switch (type) {
            case EMAIL -> new EmailChannel();
            case SMS -> new SmsChannel();
        };
    }
}

// ---------- 2. Registry factory: new types without editing this class ----------
final class ChannelRegistry {
    private final Map<String, Supplier<NotificationChannel>> creators = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    void register(String key, Supplier<NotificationChannel> creator) {
        if (creators.putIfAbsent(key, creator) != null) {   // atomic duplicate check
            throw new IllegalStateException("Channel already registered: " + key);
        }
    }

    NotificationChannel create(String key) {
        Supplier<NotificationChannel> creator = creators.get(key);
        if (creator == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown channel: " + key);
        return creator.get();
    }
}

// ---------- 3. Factory Method: base class owns the workflow, subclass picks the product ----------
abstract class OrderNotifier {
    protected abstract NotificationChannel createChannel();   // the factory method

    final String notifyShipped(String userId, String orderId) {
        return createChannel().send(userId, "Order " + orderId + " shipped");
    }
}

final class EmailOrderNotifier extends OrderNotifier {
    protected NotificationChannel createChannel() { return new EmailChannel(); }
}

// ---------- 4. Abstract Factory: a family whose members must match ----------
interface PaymentClient { String charge(String orderId, long amountMinor); }
interface WebhookVerifier { boolean verify(String payload, String signature); }

interface PaymentProviderKit {
    PaymentClient paymentClient();
    WebhookVerifier webhookVerifier();
}

final class AcmePayKit implements PaymentProviderKit {
    public PaymentClient paymentClient() {
        return (orderId, amount) -> "acme_txn_" + orderId + "_" + amount;
    }
    public WebhookVerifier webhookVerifier() {
        // Stand-in for HMAC verification with AcmePay's scheme.
        return (payload, sig) -> sig.equals("acme:" + payload.length());
    }
}

final class ZetaPayKit implements PaymentProviderKit {
    public PaymentClient paymentClient() {
        return (orderId, amount) -> "ZP-" + orderId + "-" + amount;
    }
    public WebhookVerifier webhookVerifier() {
        return (payload, sig) -> sig.equals("zeta-" + payload.length());
    }
}

final class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentClient client;
    private final WebhookVerifier verifier;

    CheckoutService(PaymentProviderKit kit) {   // both come from ONE kit: they cannot mismatch
        this.client = kit.paymentClient();
        this.verifier = kit.webhookVerifier();
    }

    String pay(String orderId, long amountMinor) { return client.charge(orderId, amountMinor); }
    boolean onWebhook(String payload, String signature) { return verifier.verify(payload, signature); }
}

public class FactoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(SimpleChannelFactory.create(ChannelType.SMS).send("u42", "Seat A7 confirmed"));

        ChannelRegistry registry = new ChannelRegistry();
        registry.register("EMAIL", EmailChannel::new);
        // Follow-up "add WhatsApp": a registration, no edits to ChannelRegistry.
        registry.register("WHATSAPP", () -> (userId, msg) -> "WHATSAPP to " + userId + ": " + msg);
        System.out.println(registry.create("WHATSAPP").send("u42", "Seat A7 confirmed"));
        try {
            registry.create("PIGEON");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        System.out.println(new EmailOrderNotifier().notifyShipped("u42", "o-9001"));

        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(new ZetaPayKit());   // chosen by merchant config
        System.out.println(checkout.pay("o-9001", 37000));
        System.out.println("webhook valid = " + checkout.onWebhook("{\"status\":\"paid\"}", "zeta-17"));
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — in Python a class is already a callable factory, so a dict from key to class is the registry. A decorator makes registration declarative.

# File: factory_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable, Dict, Protocol


class NotificationChannel(Protocol):
    def send(self, user_id: str, message: str) -> str: ...


class EmailChannel:
    def send(self, user_id: str, message: str) -> str:
        return f"EMAIL to {user_id}: {message}"


class SmsChannel:
    def send(self, user_id: str, message: str) -> str:
        return f"SMS to {user_id}: {message}"


class ChannelType(Enum):
    EMAIL = "EMAIL"
    SMS = "SMS"


# ---------- 1. Simple factory: dict dispatch instead of if/elif ----------
_SIMPLE = {ChannelType.EMAIL: EmailChannel, ChannelType.SMS: SmsChannel}


def create_channel(channel_type: ChannelType) -> NotificationChannel:
    return _SIMPLE[channel_type]()   # KeyError on a missing type: no silent default


# ---------- 2. Registry factory with a registration decorator ----------
class ChannelRegistry:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._creators: Dict[str, Callable[[], NotificationChannel]] = {}

    def register(self, key: str) -> Callable[[type], type]:
        def decorator(cls: type) -> type:
            if key in self._creators:
                raise ValueError(f"Channel already registered: {key}")
            self._creators[key] = cls
            return cls
        return decorator

    def create(self, key: str) -> NotificationChannel:
        try:
            return self._creators[key]()
        except KeyError:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown channel: {key}") from None


registry = ChannelRegistry()
registry.register("EMAIL")(EmailChannel)


@registry.register("WHATSAPP")   # follow-up "add WhatsApp": declared next to the class, no edits elsewhere
class WhatsAppChannel:
    def send(self, user_id: str, message: str) -> str:
        return f"WHATSAPP to {user_id}: {message}"


# ---------- 3. Factory Method ----------
class OrderNotifier(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def create_channel(self) -> NotificationChannel: ...

    def notify_shipped(self, user_id: str, order_id: str) -> str:
        return self.create_channel().send(user_id, f"Order {order_id} shipped")


class EmailOrderNotifier(OrderNotifier):
    def create_channel(self) -> NotificationChannel:
        return EmailChannel()


# ---------- 4. Abstract Factory ----------
class PaymentProviderKit(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def payment_client(self) -> Callable[[str, int], str]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def webhook_verifier(self) -> Callable[[str, str], bool]: ...


class ZetaPayKit(PaymentProviderKit):
    def payment_client(self) -> Callable[[str, int], str]:
        return lambda order_id, amount: f"ZP-{order_id}-{amount}"

    def webhook_verifier(self) -> Callable[[str, str], bool]:
        return lambda payload, sig: sig == f"zeta-{len(payload)}"   # stand-in for HMAC


class CheckoutService:
    def __init__(self, kit: PaymentProviderKit) -> None:
        self._charge = kit.payment_client()      # both from one kit -> they match
        self._verify = kit.webhook_verifier()

    def pay(self, order_id: str, amount_minor: int) -> str:
        return self._charge(order_id, amount_minor)

    def on_webhook(self, payload: str, signature: str) -> bool:
        return self._verify(payload, signature)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(create_channel(ChannelType.SMS).send("u42", "Seat A7 confirmed"))
    print(registry.create("WHATSAPP").send("u42", "Seat A7 confirmed"))
    try:
        registry.create("PIGEON")
    except ValueError as e:
        print("Rejected:", e)
    print(EmailOrderNotifier().notify_shipped("u42", "o-9001"))

    checkout = CheckoutService(ZetaPayKit())
    print(checkout.pay("o-9001", 37000))
    print("webhook valid =", checkout.on_webhook('{"status":"paid"}', "zeta-17"))

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 Input: ChannelType.SMS, user "u42", message "Seat A7 confirmed"
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] SimpleChannelFactory.create(SMS)     → switch → new SmsChannel()
    ▼
🎯 [2] send("u42", ...)                     → "SMS to u42: Seat A7 confirmed"

📥 Input: key "WHATSAPP"
    ▼
🧮 [3] registry.create("WHATSAPP")          → map lookup hit → Supplier.get() → WhatsApp channel
🎯 [4] send                                 → "WHATSAPP to u42: Seat A7 confirmed"

📥 Input: key "PIGEON"
    ▼
❌ [5] registry.create("PIGEON")            → map lookup miss → IllegalArgumentException "Unknown channel: PIGEON"

📥 Input: merchant configured ZetaPayKit, order "o-9001", 37000 minor units (₹370.00)
    ▼
⚙️ [6] new CheckoutService(kit)             → client AND verifier both taken from ZetaPayKit
🎯 [7] pay                                  → "ZP-o-9001-37000"
🎯 [8] onWebhook('{"status":"paid"}', "zeta-17") → payload length 17 → true

  1. Step 1 is the only line in the program that names SmsChannel outside its own file. That's the whole point.

  2. Steps 3–4 added a channel with zero edits to ChannelRegistry. The price is step 5: an unknown key can only fail at runtime, which is why you validate configured keys at startup.

  3. Step 6 is Abstract Factory's guarantee. CheckoutService has no way to receive an AcmePay verifier alongside a ZetaPay client.

  4. Money travels as long minor units (37000 paise) across the provider boundary, which is how payment APIs typically expect it (→ item 37).

9. When TO Use This

  • You're about to switch on a type code to construct something — vehicle types, spot sizes, channels, document parsers.

  • Creation needs configuration or dependencies the caller shouldn't know about (API keys, pools, retry policy).

  • New variants arrive from outside your code — plugins, partner teams, config-driven types → registry.

  • Several objects must be used as a matched set — a provider's client + webhook verifier + refund client, or a theme's widgets → Abstract Factory.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • Only one concrete class exists and none is on the horizon. new ParkingTicket(...) is fine; a TicketFactory for it is ceremony (→ item 26).

  • The caller legitimately knows the concrete type. A test building new SmsChannel() directly is clearer than going through a factory.

  • You'd need an Abstract Factory with one family. That's just an interface with two methods; name the family when the second one arrives.

  • The DI container already does it. In Spring, a Map<String, NotificationChannel> injected by bean name is a registry; hand-rolling another is duplication.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "List.of(...) and Optional.of(...) are the Factory Method pattern."

Reality: Those are static factory methods — named constructors (Effective Java, Item 1). GoF Factory Method is an overridable instance method a base class calls so subclasses pick the product. Same word, different pattern; interviewers use the confusion as a probe.

Misconception: "A simple factory makes the code open/closed."

Reality: It centralises the switch; adding a type still edits the factory. Only a registry (or the DI container) makes creation open to extension without modification.

Personal misconception (held before learning): TODO — add one you actually held. Not invented here, per the template's no-fabrication rule.

12. Interview Traps

Reciting all three GoF variants without saying which the problem needs. The interviewer wants the choice, not the catalogue.

A factory with a default -> branch that returns something. A silent fallback turns a missing type into wrong behaviour instead of an error.

Creating heavyweight products per call. A factory returning a new HTTP-client-backed channel on every notification is a connection leak with a pattern name.

Calling it Abstract Factory when there is one product. That's a simple factory; the misuse of the name signals memorisation.

Forgetting where the factory itself comes from. If the factory is a static global, you've rebuilt the Singleton testability problem (→ item 16). Inject it.

13. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Skipped — no defensible, citable benchmarks for this topic; per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented numbers.

14. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
Latency Negligible — a switch or a hash lookup. The real cost is what the product's constructor does.
Safety Exhaustive switch gives compile-time safety; registry trades it for runtime openness.
Extensibility Registry and Abstract Factory are open; simple factory is closed but centralised.
Ops complexity Registries need startup validation and a way to list registered keys when debugging.
Testability Business code takes a factory interface, so tests inject one that returns fakes.

15. Real World Usage

JDK: javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory (an abstract factory selected at runtime); java.util.ServiceLoader (the plugin registry mechanism); Calendar.getInstance() and NumberFormat.getInstance() as static factories.

Spring: BeanFactory is a factory for every bean; FactoryBean<T> lets you plug custom creation logic into it; injecting Map<String, SomeInterface> gives you a registry for free.

Python stdlib: logging.getLogger(name) is a factory that caches one logger per name; collections.namedtuple is a class factory.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The form to prefer in Java? Single-element enum — serialization- and reflection-safe for free.
Lazy without locks? Holder idiom: static nested class, initialised by the JVM on first access.
Why does DCL need volatile? Reference can be published before construction finishes; volatile forbids seeing that.
The design objection? A static accessor is a hidden, un-injectable dependency — tests can't substitute it.
The senior answer? One instance, created at the composition root and injected. Singleton scope, not Singleton pattern.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

A singleton guarantees one instance of a class. In Java I'd write it as a single-element enum, or the holder idiom if it must be lazy — both are thread-safe without explicit locks. If they ask for double-checked locking, the instance field must be volatile, otherwise another thread can see a half-constructed object. But my design answer is usually different: I want one instance, not a global accessor. I create it once at startup and inject it, which keeps it testable. That distinction is what the question is really about.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why is double-checked locking broken without volatile?

Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up whenever Singleton comes up in a Java loop.

Really testing: whether you understand safe publication, not whether you memorised the idiom.

instance = new Config() is not atomic. It allocates memory, runs the constructor, and assigns the reference — and the JIT is allowed to assign the reference before the constructor has finished writing fields. Thread A, inside the lock, does that. Thread B, on the unsynchronised first check, sees instance != null, skips the lock, and uses an object whose fields are still defaults.

Marking the field volatile establishes a happens-before relationship for reads of that field, which (since Java 5's memory model) forbids B from observing the reference before construction is complete. The holder idiom avoids the whole question: the JVM's class-initialisation lock guarantees Holder.INSTANCE is fully constructed before any thread can read it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Enum singleton, holder idiom, or "just inject one instance" — how do you choose?

Really testing: whether you see Singleton as a testability decision, not a syntax one.

If the object is a stateless utility or a true process-wide resource with no reason to substitute it in tests — an ID generator backed by an AtomicLong, a metrics registry — the enum form is the safest and shortest. Use the holder idiom when construction is expensive and must be lazy, or when the class must extend something (enums can't).

For anything with dependencies or behaviour a test would want to control — a clock, a config source, a payment client — don't use a global accessor at all. Create one instance at the composition root and pass it through constructors. You still have exactly one instance at runtime; you've just stopped letting every class reach out and grab it. That's what Spring's default singleton scope does, and it's why Spring beans are testable while hand-rolled getInstance() calls are not.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Name the ways a "singleton" ends up with two instances.

Reflection can call a private constructor (setAccessible(true)); the holder and DCL forms need a constructor guard that throws on a second call, while enum constructors can't be invoked reflectively at all. Serialization creates a new instance on readObject unless you add readResolve() returning the singleton; enums are serialised by name and are immune. Multiple class loaders — two web apps in one container, or a plugin loader — each load the class separately and get their own "singleton".

And the one that matters most at scale: multiple processes. A singleton is one per JVM. Ten service replicas have ten IdGenerators producing colliding IDs. Anything that must be unique across the fleet — IDs, rate limits, leases — needs a distributed mechanism (a database sequence, Snowflake-style node IDs, Redis), and saying so is the bridge from LLD to HLD.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

An in-process RateLimiterRegistry is a singleton today. Redesign it for testability and for a 20-replica deployment.

Really testing: whether you can separate "one per process" from "one global truth" and pick the boundary.

Step one is removing the static accessor: RateLimiterRegistry becomes an interface, the in-memory implementation is constructed once at startup and injected into the filter that uses it. Tests now inject a fake that always allows or always denies, and the time source is an injected Clock so token refill is deterministic in tests (→ item 38).

Step two is the fleet: per-replica limits multiply the effective limit by 20. Either accept that and divide the configured limit by the replica count (cheap, drifts during autoscaling), or back the interface with a shared store — a Redis implementation doing atomic token-bucket updates in a Lua script. Because callers depend on the interface, this is a new implementation, not an edit.

Monitor the shared store's latency and error rate first, and decide the failure policy explicitly: fail-open (allow traffic if Redis is down) protects availability, fail-closed protects the backend. Not deciding is how a cache outage becomes a full outage.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Form Thread-safe Lazy Reflection-safe Serialization-safe Testable
Enum (on class load) global
Holder idiom needs guard needs readResolve global
DCL + volatile needs guard needs readResolve global
DCL without volatile broken
synchronized getInstance() global, lock on every call
Injected single instance depends on class at startup n/a n/a

DEPTH BLOCK

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Double-checked locking — the race volatile prevents:

Holder idiom — why it needs no lock: the JVM initialises a class at most once, under an internal initialisation lock, on first active use (JLS §12.4). Holder is not touched until getInstance() reads Holder.INSTANCE, so creation is lazy; and because class initialisation is serialised by the JVM, it is thread-safe with no code of yours.

Enum singleton — why it's immune: enum constants are created during enum class initialisation (same guarantee), serialised by name so deserialisation returns the existing constant, and the reflection API refuses to instantiate enum types.

6. Why It Matters in Production

Singletons show up as ID generators, config holders, connection pools, metrics registries and caches. Two things go wrong in practice. The obvious one is a racy lazy initialiser creating two pools or two caches under startup load — rare, hard to reproduce, and expensive. The common one is testability: code that calls PaymentClient.getInstance() can't be unit-tested without hitting the real client or resorting to static mocking, so it doesn't get tested. Choosing "one instance, injected" over "global accessor" is what keeps the critical path covered.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — the three correct forms, a concurrency check that proves one instance under contention, and the injected alternative.

// File: SingletonDemo.java
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.IdentityHashMap;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

// ---------- 1. Enum singleton: the default choice ----------
enum IdGenerator {
    INSTANCE;
    private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(1000);
    long nextId() { return next.getAndIncrement(); }   // atomic, no lock
}

// ---------- 2. Holder idiom: lazy, lock-free, relies on JVM class init ----------
final class AppConfig {
    private final String region;

    private AppConfig() {
        if (Holder.created) throw new IllegalStateException("use getInstance()");   // reflection guard
        this.region = "ap-south-1";   // imagine an expensive load here
    }

    private static final class Holder {
        static boolean created;
        static final AppConfig INSTANCE = create();
        private static AppConfig create() { AppConfig c = new AppConfig(); created = true; return c; }
    }

    static AppConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // triggers Holder init on first call only
    String region() { return region; }
}

// ---------- 3. Double-checked locking: only if asked, and with volatile ----------
final class ConnectionRegistry {
    private static volatile ConnectionRegistry instance;   // volatile is NOT optional

    private ConnectionRegistry() {}

    static ConnectionRegistry getInstance() {
        ConnectionRegistry local = instance;          // one volatile read on the fast path
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (ConnectionRegistry.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new ConnectionRegistry();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

// ---------- 4. The design answer: one instance, injected ----------
interface Ids { long nextId(); }

final class BookingService {
    private final Ids ids;                                   // dependency is visible and replaceable
    BookingService(Ids ids) { this.ids = ids; }
    String book(String seat) { return "booking-" + ids.nextId() + "-" + seat; }
}

public class SingletonDemo {
    // Hammer a getInstance() from many threads released at once; count distinct identities.
    static <T> int distinctInstances(Supplier<T> getter) throws InterruptedException {
        Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()));
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
            pool.submit(() -> { start.await(); seen.add(getter.get()); return null; });
        }
        start.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        return seen.size();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("enum ids: " + IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId() + ", " + IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId());
        System.out.println("holder distinct instances = " + distinctInstances(AppConfig::getInstance));
        System.out.println("DCL distinct instances    = " + distinctInstances(ConnectionRegistry::getInstance));
        System.out.println("region = " + AppConfig.getInstance().region());

        // Composition root: production wires the real generator...
        BookingService prod = new BookingService(IdGenerator.INSTANCE::nextId);
        System.out.println(prod.book("A7"));
        // ...a test wires a deterministic fake. No static mocking needed.
        BookingService test = new BookingService(() -> 42L);
        System.out.println(test.book("A7"));

        assert distinctInstances(AppConfig::getInstance) == 1;
        assert test.book("B1").equals("booking-42-B1");
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — the idiomatic singleton is a module-level instance (modules are imported once per interpreter). If a class must enforce it, the check-then-create needs a lock: the GIL does not make if instance is None: instance = ... atomic.

# File: singleton_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from typing import Callable, Optional


# ---------- 1. Idiomatic: a module-level instance ----------
class _IdGenerator:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._counter = itertools.count(1000)
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def next_id(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:                       # next() on a shared iterator is not a documented atomic op
            return next(self._counter)


id_generator = _IdGenerator()                 # importers share this one object


# ---------- 2. Class-enforced, thread-safe, lazy (double-checked with a lock) ----------
class AppConfig:
    _instance: Optional["AppConfig"] = None
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        raise RuntimeError("use AppConfig.instance()")

    @classmethod
    def instance(cls) -> "AppConfig":
        if cls._instance is None:              # fast path, no lock
            with cls._lock:
                if cls._instance is None:      # re-check: another thread may have won
                    obj = object.__new__(cls)  # bypass the guarded __init__
                    obj.region = "ap-south-1"
                    cls._instance = obj
        return cls._instance


# ---------- 3. The design answer: inject one instance ----------
class BookingService:
    def __init__(self, next_id: Callable[[], int]) -> None:
        self._next_id = next_id

    def book(self, seat: str) -> str:
        return f"booking-{self._next_id()}-{seat}"


def distinct_instances(getter: Callable[[], object]) -> int:
    start = threading.Barrier(32)

    def worker() -> int:
        start.wait()                           # release all threads together
        return id(getter())

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32) as pool:
        futures = [pool.submit(worker) for _ in range(32)]
        return len({f.result() for f in futures})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("module ids:", id_generator.next_id(), id_generator.next_id())
    print("AppConfig distinct instances =", distinct_instances(AppConfig.instance))
    print("region =", AppConfig.instance().region)

    prod = BookingService(id_generator.next_id)
    print(prod.book("A7"))
    test = BookingService(lambda: 42)          # the test double
    print(test.book("A7"))

    assert distinct_instances(AppConfig.instance) == 1
    assert test.book("B1") == "booking-42-B1"

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 main starts; no singleton class has been initialised yet
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId() ×2  → enum class init creates INSTANCE → 1000, 1001
    │
    ▼
🧵 [2] 1,000 tasks on 32 threads call AppConfig.getInstance() at once
    │      first read of Holder.INSTANCE → JVM initialises Holder exactly once
    │      every other thread blocks on the class-init lock, then reads the same reference
    ▼
🎯 [3] distinct identities collected       → 1
    │
    ▼
🧵 [4] same test on ConnectionRegistry (DCL + volatile) → 1
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [5] new BookingService(IdGenerator.INSTANCE::nextId).book("A7") → "booking-1002-A7"
    │
    ▼
🧪 [6] new BookingService(() -> 42L).book("A7")                   → "booking-42-A7"

  1. Step 1 creates the enum instance during class initialisation, so there is no laziness — acceptable because an AtomicLong is cheap.

  2. Step 2 is the holder idiom's whole argument: the JVM, not your code, guarantees one initialisation, so there is no synchronized in AppConfig.

  3. Steps 3–4 check identity with an IdentityHashMap-backed set, not equals, because two distinct instances could compare equal.

  4. Steps 5–6 are the design point. BookingService never names IdGenerator, so the test in step 6 needs no static mocking to get a deterministic ID.

9. When TO Use This

  • The object represents a genuinely process-wide resource — a metrics registry, an ID generator for in-process use, a JVM-wide cache.

  • Construction is expensive and must happen once — loading a large config or model file.

  • You're asked to implement it in the interview. Write the enum or holder form, then state the injection alternative unprompted.

  • As a scope, almost always: one instance of each service wired at the composition root is the default in any DI design.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • The class has collaborators a test would want to replace — clients, clocks, repositories. A global accessor hides the dependency and blocks substitution.

  • "One instance" must hold across processes. A JVM singleton is per process and per class loader; fleet-wide uniqueness needs a shared store.

  • It holds mutable request- or user-specific state. That's global mutable state with a pattern name, and a data leak between requests in a web server.

  • You're using it to avoid passing a parameter. That's the Service Locator smell; the parameter is the honest design.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "synchronized on the second check is enough; volatile is just an optimisation."

Reality: Without volatile, the unsynchronised first read can observe a reference to an object whose constructor hasn't finished. volatile is what makes the pattern correct, not faster.

Misconception: "Python's GIL makes a lazy singleton thread-safe."

Reality: The GIL serialises bytecodes, not your check-then-act. A thread switch between if cls._instance is None and the assignment lets two threads both create an instance. Use a lock, or a module-level instance created at import.

Personal misconception (held before learning): TODO — add one you actually held. Not invented here, per the template's no-fabrication rule.

12. Interview Traps

Writing DCL without volatile. The single most-checked detail; the interviewer will ask "is this thread-safe?" and wait.

Not mentioning testability. Implementing a perfect singleton without saying why you'd usually inject one instead reads as mid-level.

Claiming a singleton is unique "in the system." It's unique per JVM and class loader. Say "per process."

Making getInstance() fully synchronized and stopping there. Correct but takes a lock on every call; know the holder idiom as the lock-free lazy form.

Putting mutable shared state in it without thread-safety. One instance shared by all threads means every field is contended (→ §4 Concurrency).

13. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Skipped — no defensible, citable benchmarks for this topic; per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented numbers.

14. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
Latency Enum and holder: no lock on access. synchronized getInstance(): a lock on every call. DCL: one volatile read.
🧵 Concurrency One shared instance means all its mutable state is contended — thread-safety moves into the class.
Testability Global accessor blocks substitution; injection restores it at zero runtime cost.
Scale Per JVM only. Horizontal scaling silently multiplies "the" singleton.
Ops complexity Hidden global state makes startup order and hot reload harder to reason about.

15. Real World Usage

JDK: Runtime.getRuntime() is the textbook eager singleton; Collections.emptyList() returns a shared immutable instance.

Spring: beans are singleton-scoped by default — one instance per container, injected rather than looked up — which is the testable form of the idea. See Bean Scopes.

Python: modules themselves are singletons (cached in sys.modules); None, True and False are singleton objects compared with is.

  • ../04-concurrency-in-lld/30-concurrenthashmap-atomics.md — atomic primitives used inside shared instances.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • ../05-modeling-craft/38-time-as-an-injected-dependency.md — the Clock is the most common "singleton" that must be injectable.

  • 26-pattern-overuse.md — singleton abuse is the most-cited overuse case.

Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Singleton scope in a DI container — choose it whenever the instance has dependencies or needs test substitution.

  • Distributed coordination (DB sequence, Redis, leases) — choose it when uniqueness must hold across processes.

Composes with
