notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Observer — intent, structure, push vs pull — Observer Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Observer, with the subscription-management detail — Observer (refactoring.guru)

  • Why java.util.Observer is deprecated — Observer (Java SE 17 API)

  • Publisher decoupled from subscribers via one channel — Martin Fowler: Event Aggregator

  • Bonus — the JDK's reactive-streams interfaces with backpressure: Flow (Java SE 17 API)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/behavioral.md. This note is the LLD-round layer with runnable code.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What varies? Who reacts to an event. The publisher never changes when a reaction is added.
Sync vs async dispatch — the cost of each? Sync: slow listener slows publisher. Async: ordering and delivery become your problem.
One listener throws — what must happen? Others still run; the publishing operation still succeeds. Catch and log per listener.
Safe listener collection for concurrent subscribe/publish? CopyOnWriteArrayList — reads dominate; iteration never sees ConcurrentModificationException.
The memory leak? Lapsed listener: never unsubscribed, so the subject keeps it alive. Return an unsubscribe handle.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Observer lets one object announce that something happened while an open-ended set of others react, without the announcer knowing who they are. In BookMyShow, when a seat is booked, the seat map refreshes, the waitlist is notified and analytics records it — and BookingService only publishes a SeatEvent. Adding SMS alerts is a new listener, no edit. The two things I'd make explicit are whether dispatch is synchronous or asynchronous, and that one failing listener can't break the booking or the other listeners.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Push or pull — what goes in the event?

In the push model, the event carries the data the listeners need (showId, seatId, new status). In the pull model, the event carries a reference and listeners call back into the subject for details. Push decouples listeners from the subject's API and works across threads; pull keeps events small but couples every listener to the subject and invites reading state that has already changed again.

For LLD, push an immutable event record. Immutability matters as soon as dispatch is async or listeners run on different threads: a mutable event shared by three listeners is a data race.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Synchronous or asynchronous dispatch for seat-status events?

Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up once an observer is drawn in BookMyShow or elevator-display designs.

Really testing: whether you know async isn't free — it trades latency for ordering and delivery guarantees.

Synchronous dispatch is simple and ordered: listeners run on the booking thread, in registration order, and when publish() returns, every listener has run. The cost is that booking latency is now the sum of listener latencies — one slow analytics call makes seat booking slow.

Asynchronous dispatch fixes latency but creates three new problems. Ordering: "HELD then BOOKED" can arrive reversed on a thread pool, so either use a single-threaded executor per key (per show) or put a version number in the event. Delivery: if the process dies after the booking commits but before the executor runs the task, the event is lost — in-process async is at-most-once. Backpressure: an unbounded queue behind slow listeners grows until memory runs out. My usual answer is sync for cheap in-memory listeners that must be consistent (seat map), async for slow side effects (notifications), and "in production that's an outbox table plus a queue" in one sentence for anything that must not be lost.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

A listener unsubscribes itself inside its own callback. What happens?

With a plain ArrayList and a for-each loop, the removal during iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException — and the same happens if another thread subscribes mid-publish. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, so self-removal is safe and the listener simply isn't called on the next event. The trade is that every subscribe copies the array, which is right for the read-heavy "subscribe rarely, publish often" shape and wrong if listeners churn per request.

The related leak: a listener object registered by a short-lived component (a user's screen, a request) and never removed stays reachable from the subject forever. Returning an AutoCloseable subscription handle makes unsubscribing explicit and usable in try-with-resources.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Seat events must reach 50,000 connected clients across 40 app servers. Evolve this design.

Really testing: whether you can place the in-process Observer inside a distributed fan-out without pretending it scales on its own.

The constraint is that a booking on server 7 must reach clients connected to all 40 servers, and a hot show generates bursts. The in-process event bus stays — it's still how the booking code announces the event — but one of its listeners becomes a publisher to a broker topic partitioned by showId, which keeps per-show ordering.

Each app server subscribes to the topic and fans out to its locally connected WebSocket clients by show. Clients get a version number per seat so a reconnect can fetch a snapshot and discard stale events. To avoid losing events between database commit and broker publish, the booking writes to an outbox table in the same transaction and a relay publishes from it.

The first metric to watch is consumer lag per partition: a hot show's partition lagging means clients see seats as available that are already booked, which surfaces as a spike in "seat no longer available" errors at checkout.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Observer (in-process) Event bus / aggregator Message broker (Kafka, SQS) Reactive streams (Flow)
Coupling Listener knows the subject Both know only the bus Both know only the topic Publisher/subscriber contract
Delivery Sync or in-memory async Same as observer Durable, at-least-once In-memory, demand-driven
Ordering Registration order (sync) Per bus policy Per partition Per subscription
Backpressure None None Consumer pull request(n)
Scope One object's events One process Across services One process
LLD answer? Name it, don't build it Rarely

DEPTH BLOCK

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

The five rules that make it production-shaped:

  • Publish after the state change commits. Listeners must never observe an event for a change that later rolls back.

  • Immutable events. A record in Java, a frozen dataclass in Python.

  • Snapshot iteration. Subscribe/unsubscribe during publish must not throw or skip listeners.

  • Per-listener exception isolation. Catch around each call, log with the listener's name, continue.

  • Explicit subscription lifetime. subscribe() returns a handle whose close() unsubscribes.

6. Why It Matters in Production

Side effects accumulate around core operations: a booking eventually needs a seat-map refresh, email, SMS, loyalty points, analytics, fraud scoring and a cache invalidation. Written inline, book() grows to eight responsibilities, each a reason for the critical path to fail or slow down. With Observer, the core operation stays small and each side effect is an independently deployable, independently failing listener. The same seam later becomes the outbox-to-broker boundary, so the in-process design migrates to a distributed one without rewriting the booking code.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — a typed event bus with snapshot iteration, per-listener isolation, unsubscribe handles, and an async variant that preserves order.

// File: ObserverDemo.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

enum SeatStatus { HELD, BOOKED, RELEASED }

// Push model: the event carries what listeners need, and is immutable.
record SeatEvent(String showId, String seatId, SeatStatus status) {}

@FunctionalInterface
interface SeatListener {
    void onEvent(SeatEvent event);
}

final class EventBus {
    private final List<SeatListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();   // snapshot iteration

    /** Returns a handle; closing it unsubscribes. Prevents the lapsed-listener leak. */
    AutoCloseable subscribe(SeatListener listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
        return () -> listeners.remove(listener);
    }

    /** Synchronous: when this returns, every listener has run, in registration order. */
    void publish(SeatEvent event) {
        for (SeatListener listener : listeners) {
            try {
                listener.onEvent(event);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {   // one bad listener must not break the others or the publisher
                System.out.println("  [bus] listener failed on " + event.seatId() + ": " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}

/** Async decorator over the bus. Single thread => events are delivered in publish order. */
final class AsyncEventBus implements AutoCloseable {
    private final EventBus delegate;
    private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

    AsyncEventBus(EventBus delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    void publish(SeatEvent event) { executor.execute(() -> delegate.publish(event)); }

    @Override
    public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        executor.shutdown();                                  // stop accepting, drain what's queued
        if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) executor.shutdownNow();
    }
}

final class BookingService {
    private final EventBus bus;
    BookingService(EventBus bus) { this.bus = bus; }

    void book(String showId, String seatId) {
        // ... atomic seat state change happens here first (-> item 28) ...
        System.out.println("booked " + seatId);
        bus.publish(new SeatEvent(showId, seatId, SeatStatus.BOOKED));   // publish AFTER commit
    }
}

public class ObserverDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus();
        bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("  seat map: " + e.seatId() + " -> " + e.status()));
        AutoCloseable waitlist = bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("  waitlist: notify watchers of " + e.showId()));
        bus.subscribe(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("analytics endpoint down"); });

        BookingService booking = new BookingService(bus);
        booking.book("show-42", "A7");        // analytics fails; booking and other listeners unaffected

        waitlist.close();                     // unsubscribe via handle
        booking.book("show-42", "A8");        // waitlist no longer called

        try (AsyncEventBus async = new AsyncEventBus(bus)) {
            async.publish(new SeatEvent("show-42", "B1", SeatStatus.HELD));
            async.publish(new SeatEvent("show-42", "B1", SeatStatus.BOOKED));   // same thread -> same order
            System.out.println("publisher returned; async listeners may still be running");
        }                                     // close() drains the queue
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same design. Iterating over a tuple snapshot gives the same safety as CopyOnWriteArrayList.

# File: observer_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable, List

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="  [bus] %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("bus")


class SeatStatus(Enum):
    HELD = "HELD"
    BOOKED = "BOOKED"
    RELEASED = "RELEASED"


@dataclass(frozen=True)          # immutable event: safe to hand to other threads
class SeatEvent:
    show_id: str
    seat_id: str
    status: SeatStatus


SeatListener = Callable[[SeatEvent], None]


class EventBus:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._listeners: List[SeatListener] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def subscribe(self, listener: SeatListener) -> Callable[[], None]:
        with self._lock:
            self._listeners.append(listener)

        def unsubscribe() -> None:
            with self._lock:
                if listener in self._listeners:
                    self._listeners.remove(listener)

        return unsubscribe

    def publish(self, event: SeatEvent) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            snapshot = tuple(self._listeners)      # iterate a snapshot, outside the lock
        for listener in snapshot:
            try:
                listener(event)
            except Exception as exc:               # isolate each listener
                log.warning("listener failed on %s: %s", event.seat_id, exc)


class AsyncEventBus:
    def __init__(self, delegate: EventBus) -> None:
        self._delegate = delegate
        self._executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)   # one worker keeps publish order

    def publish(self, event: SeatEvent) -> None:
        self._executor.submit(self._delegate.publish, event)

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._executor.shutdown(wait=True)                    # drain queued events


class BookingService:
    def __init__(self, bus: EventBus) -> None:
        self._bus = bus

    def book(self, show_id: str, seat_id: str) -> None:
        print(f"booked {seat_id}")
        self._bus.publish(SeatEvent(show_id, seat_id, SeatStatus.BOOKED))


def failing_analytics(event: SeatEvent) -> None:
    raise RuntimeError("analytics endpoint down")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bus = EventBus()
    bus.subscribe(lambda e: print(f"  seat map: {e.seat_id} -> {e.status.value}"))
    unsubscribe_waitlist = bus.subscribe(lambda e: print(f"  waitlist: notify watchers of {e.show_id}"))
    bus.subscribe(failing_analytics)

    booking = BookingService(bus)
    booking.book("show-42", "A7")

    unsubscribe_waitlist()
    booking.book("show-42", "A8")

    async_bus = AsyncEventBus(bus)
    async_bus.publish(SeatEvent("show-42", "B1", SeatStatus.HELD))
    async_bus.publish(SeatEvent("show-42", "B1", SeatStatus.BOOKED))
    async_bus.close()

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 Listeners registered: [seatMap, waitlist, analytics(throws)]
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] book("show-42", "A7")                    → prints "booked A7" (state committed first)
    ▼
📡 [2] publish(SeatEvent(show-42, A7, BOOKED))   → snapshot = [seatMap, waitlist, analytics]
    ├─▶ ✅ seatMap   → "seat map: A7 -> BOOKED"
    ├─▶ ✅ waitlist  → "waitlist: notify watchers of show-42"
    └─▶ ❌ analytics → throws → caught → "[bus] listener failed on A7: analytics endpoint down"
    ▼
🎯 [3] book() returns normally                   → booking succeeded despite the failure
    ▼
⚙️ [4] waitlist.close()                          → listeners = [seatMap, analytics]
⚙️ [5] book("show-42", "A8")                     → seat map line + analytics failure, no waitlist line
    ▼
🧵 [6] async.publish(B1 HELD), async.publish(B1 BOOKED)
    │      both queued on ONE worker thread → publish() returns immediately; the worker may already be running
    ▼
🎯 [7] worker runs HELD then BOOKED               → order preserved by the single-thread executor

  1. Step 1 before step 2 is the commit-then-publish rule. If publishing came first and the seat write failed, the seat map would show a booking that doesn't exist.

  2. Step 2's snapshot means a listener unsubscribing itself mid-loop can't throw or cause a skipped neighbour.

  3. Step 3 is the isolation guarantee. The analytics outage is logged; the user's booking is unaffected.

  4. Step 7's ordering holds only because the executor has one thread. A pool of four could deliver BOOKED before HELD — say this when you draw async dispatch.

9. When TO Use This

  • An operation has side effects whose number will grow — notifications, audit, analytics, cache invalidation around a booking or order.

  • The reacting parties belong to different modules or teams, and the core code shouldn't depend on them.

  • State changes must be pushed to displays — elevator floor indicators, seat maps, dashboards.

  • You want a clean seam to later move side effects out of process (outbox → broker) without touching the core.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • The reaction is part of the same business invariant. Releasing a seat hold and refunding the payment must succeed together — that's a transaction or an explicit call, not a fire-and-forget listener.

  • Exactly one reaction exists and always will. A direct method call is clearer and easier to trace in a debugger.

  • Delivery must survive a crash. In-process observers are at-most-once; use an outbox and a durable queue.

  • Listeners depend on each other's order ("send SMS only after loyalty points are credited"). That's a workflow; model the sequence explicitly instead of relying on registration order.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Making dispatch async makes the system more reliable."

Reality: It makes the publisher faster and the delivery less reliable — a crash loses queued events, and a multi-threaded pool reorders them. Async is a latency decision that creates reliability work.

Misconception: "java.util.Observer is the Java way to do this."

Reality: It has been deprecated since Java 9 — its event model is untyped Object and it doesn't specify ordering or threading. Define your own typed listener interface, or use java.util.concurrent.Flow when backpressure matters.

Personal misconception (held before learning): TODO — add one you actually held. Not invented here, per the template's no-fabrication rule.

12. Interview Traps

Drawing the observer without saying sync or async. The follow-up is certain; pre-empt it.

No exception handling in the publish loop. The interviewer asks "what if the email listener throws?" and the honest answer is "the booking fails."

Publishing before the state change commits. Listeners then react to changes that may roll back.

Using ArrayList for listeners in a concurrent design. ConcurrentModificationException on subscribe-during-publish is the concrete bug.

Building Kafka in the LLD round. One sentence — "in production this listener writes to an outbox and a broker" — then stop. That's HLD.

13. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Skipped — no defensible, citable benchmarks for this topic; per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented numbers.

14. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
Latency Sync: publisher pays the sum of listener latencies. Async: publisher pays an enqueue.
Consistency Sync listeners see the event before publish returns; async ones see it eventually, possibly reordered.
Reliability In-process async is at-most-once; durability needs an outbox + broker.
Scale CopyOnWriteArrayList copies on every subscribe — fine for stable listener sets, bad for per-request churn.
Debuggability Control flow is implicit; log listener names and durations or "who reacted to this?" becomes unanswerable.

15. Real World Usage

JDK / Swing: ActionListener and the whole AWT/Swing event model — see Introduction to Event Listeners; PropertyChangeSupport for bean property changes.

Spring: ApplicationEventPublisher with @EventListener, and @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT), which is exactly the commit-then-publish rule as an annotation.

Python stdlib: logging handlers — a logger publishes records to every attached handler, and one handler's failure is routed to handleError rather than breaking the others.

16. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • ../02-oo-design-principles/12-interface-segregation-for-extension-points.md — a listener interface is a narrow extension point.

  • ../04-concurrency-in-lld/27-identify-the-contended-resource.md — the listener list is shared state under concurrent subscribe/publish.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • ../../07-Design-problems/book-my-show.md — seat-status broadcast.

  • ../../07-Design-problems/elevator.md — display and panel updates.

Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Direct method call — choose it when there is one reaction that is part of the same invariant.

  • Outbox + message broker — choose it when events must survive crashes or cross services.

Composes with

  • 18-state.md — state transitions are the natural events to publish.

  • 19-command.md — async dispatch queues command-like tasks.

18. System Design Application

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • State — intent and structure — State Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • State vs Strategy, with the transition diagram — State (refactoring.guru)

  • The refactoring that gets you there — Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (refactoring.com)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/behavioral.md. This note is the LLD-round layer with runnable code.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The tell that you need it? Methods that start by checking a status field, with nested ifs per status.
State vs Strategy? Same shape. Strategy is chosen from outside; State replaces itself on transitions.
Enum + guarded methods, or a class per state? Enum for few states and trivial behaviour; classes when behaviour per state grows.
Invalid transition — return false or throw? Throw a domain exception (IllegalTransitionException) — a silent false gets ignored.
Two threads transition the same object? Transitions must be atomic: lock the aggregate or CAS on a version.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

State moves "what does this object do in its current status?" out of if (status == ...) chains and into one class per state. A booking is Held, Confirmed, Expired or Cancelled; each state class implements only the transitions it allows and returns the next state. So confirm() on an expired hold fails in exactly one place, and adding a Refunded state is a new class. Two things I'd call out: transitions must be atomic under concurrency, and duplicate payment callbacks must be idempotent, not errors.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

State and Strategy have the same class diagram. What's actually different?

Seen in the wild: a common comparative probe right after either pattern is drawn.

Who changes the object's behaviour. With Strategy, a client or config chooses the algorithm and it usually stays fixed for the object's life — the pricing engine doesn't swap its own rules. With State, the object replaces its own behaviour as a consequence of handling a request: Held.confirm() returns a Confirmed, and from then on the same method calls do different things.

That's why state classes know about each other (each returns its successors) while strategies are independent of each other. If your "strategies" are returning other strategies, you've written State.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Enum with a switch, or a class per state?

Really testing: judgment about when the pattern pays for itself, not the pattern itself.

For a small machine — three states, two transitions, no per-state data — an enum plus guarded intent methods is lighter and fully readable: if (status != HELD) throw ...; status = CONFIRMED;. The transition table fits on screen, and the compiler's exhaustive switch catches a missing case.

Switch to a class per state when behaviour per state grows beyond "allowed or not": when states carry their own data (Held has a holdUntil, Confirmed has a paymentId), when each state has several methods with different logic, or when the number of states × operations makes the switch statements repeat across methods. The booking below crosses that line because Held owns the expiry check and Confirmed owns idempotency — say the reason, not just the choice.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The payment callback and the expiry sweeper hit the same booking in the same millisecond. What happens?

Without coordination, both read Held, one writes Confirmed, the other writes Expired, and the last write wins — a paid booking can end up expired and the seat resold. The transition itself must be atomic. In memory, synchronized transition methods on the Booking aggregate are enough, because the contended resource is one booking (→ item 27). In a database, it's an optimistic update: UPDATE booking SET state='CONFIRMED', version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND state='HELD' AND version=?, with zero rows updated meaning "lost the race — reload and re-decide."

The second half is idempotency. Payment providers retry callbacks, so confirm(pay_1) on a booking already Confirmed with pay_1 must succeed silently. confirm(pay_2) on it is a real conflict — a double charge — and must throw so the caller refunds. The code below implements both.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Model an e-commerce order lifecycle across order, payment and shipping services.

Really testing: whether a single in-memory state machine grows into a persisted, event-driven one without losing its invariants.

The constraint is that no single service owns all the state: payment authorises, the warehouse packs, the carrier ships. So the order service owns the order's state machine — Created → PaymentPending → Paid → Packed → Shipped → Delivered, plus Cancelled and Refunded — persisted with a version column, and other services report events that the order service maps to transitions.

Each transition is validated against the current state (the State pattern, now reading from the database row), written with an optimistic version check, and published as an event after commit via an outbox (→ item 17). A cancellation after Paid triggers a compensating refund rather than a rollback — that's the saga shape.

The metric to watch first is stuck-in-state counts: orders in PaymentPending older than the payment timeout, or Paid but not Packed after the SLA. A state machine that's correct but silently stalled is the common production failure, and only a per-state age histogram catches it.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Enum + guarded methods State pattern (class per state) Transition table (data) State-machine library
Best for ≤4 states, trivial behaviour Per-state data and logic Many states, uniform behaviour Complex, nested, audited workflows
Adding a state Edit enum + every switch New class, edit predecessors New table rows Config
Per-state data Awkward (nullable fields) natural Varies
Readability of the full graph one place Spread across classes one table diagram tooling
Interview default Vending machine, simple seat Booking, elevator, ATM Rarely Name it, don't use it

DEPTH BLOCK

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

The booking state graph (terminal states in red):

The mechanics:

  • Context (Booking) holds a reference to the current state and delegates every operation to it. It has no if on status.

  • State interface (BookingState) declares every operation. Default implementations reject the operation — so each state only overrides what it allows, and a forgotten transition fails loudly instead of silently doing nothing.

  • Concrete states return the next state. The context assigns it. That's the only way state changes — no public setter (→ item 10).

  • Lazy expiry on access: before any operation, the context asks the state to expireIfDue(now). A background sweeper can call the same method; either path is correct (→ item 33).

  • Time is a parameter (Instant now), so expiry is deterministic in tests (→ item 38).

6. Why It Matters in Production

Lifecycle bugs are expensive bugs: a booking confirmed after its hold expired and the seat resold, an order shipped after cancellation, a refund issued twice. They come from status checks scattered across services — one code path forgets to check, or checks the wrong set of states. The State pattern puts the allowed-transition rules in one class per state, so the full graph is auditable, an illegal transition is structurally impossible to perform silently, and a new state (partial refund, on-hold for fraud review) is added without re-reading every service that touches the status field.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — booking lifecycle with a sealed state hierarchy, lazy expiry, idempotent confirm, and atomic transitions.

// File: StateDemo.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

final class IllegalTransitionException extends RuntimeException {
    IllegalTransitionException(BookingState from, String action) {
        super("cannot " + action + " a booking that is " + from.label());
    }
}

// Every operation is declared here; the DEFAULT is to reject. States override only what they allow.
sealed interface BookingState permits Held, Confirmed, Expired, Cancelled {
    default BookingState confirm(String paymentId) { throw new IllegalTransitionException(this, "confirm"); }
    default BookingState cancel() { throw new IllegalTransitionException(this, "cancel"); }
    default BookingState expireIfDue(Instant now) { return this; }   // no-op unless Held: sweeper-safe
    default String label() { return getClass().getSimpleName().toUpperCase(); }
}

record Held(Instant holdUntil) implements BookingState {
    public BookingState confirm(String paymentId) { return new Confirmed(paymentId); }
    public BookingState cancel() { return new Cancelled("hold released"); }
    public BookingState expireIfDue(Instant now) {
        return now.isBefore(holdUntil) ? this : new Expired();
    }
}

record Confirmed(String paymentId) implements BookingState {
    public BookingState confirm(String retriedPaymentId) {
        if (paymentId.equals(retriedPaymentId)) return this;          // provider retry: idempotent no-op
        throw new IllegalTransitionException(this, "confirm with a second payment");   // double charge
    }
    public BookingState cancel() { return new Cancelled("refund " + paymentId); }
}

record Expired() implements BookingState {}                           // terminal: rejects everything

record Cancelled(String reason) implements BookingState {}            // terminal

// Context: holds the current state, delegates, never branches on it.
final class Booking {
    private final String id;
    private BookingState state;
    private final List<String> history = new ArrayList<>();

    Booking(String id, Instant now, Duration holdFor) {
        this.id = id;
        this.state = new Held(now.plus(holdFor));
    }

    // synchronized: the contended resource is this one booking (callback vs sweeper vs user).
    synchronized void confirm(String paymentId, Instant now) {
        apply(state.expireIfDue(now));          // lazy expiry before acting
        apply(state.confirm(paymentId));
    }

    synchronized void cancel(Instant now) {
        apply(state.expireIfDue(now));
        apply(state.cancel());
    }

    synchronized void expireIfDue(Instant now) { apply(state.expireIfDue(now)); }   // sweeper entry point

    private void apply(BookingState next) {
        if (next != state) {
            history.add(state.label() + " -> " + next.label());
            state = next;
        }
    }

    synchronized String describe() { return id + " " + state + " " + history; }
}

public class StateDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Instant t0 = Instant.parse("2026-09-16T10:00:00Z");
        Duration hold = Duration.ofMinutes(10);

        Booking b1 = new Booking("bk-1", t0, hold);
        b1.confirm("pay_1", t0.plusSeconds(180));     // paid at 10:03
        b1.confirm("pay_1", t0.plusSeconds(185));     // provider retries the callback: no-op
        b1.cancel(t0.plusSeconds(3600));              // user cancels later -> refund
        System.out.println(b1.describe());

        Booking b2 = new Booking("bk-2", t0, hold);
        try {
            b2.confirm("pay_2", t0.plusSeconds(720)); // callback at 10:12, hold ended 10:10
        } catch (IllegalTransitionException e) {
            System.out.println("bk-2 refund pay_2: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println(b2.describe());

        Booking b3 = new Booking("bk-3", t0, hold);
        b3.confirm("pay_3", t0.plusSeconds(60));
        try {
            b3.confirm("pay_9", t0.plusSeconds(90));  // a DIFFERENT payment for the same booking
        } catch (IllegalTransitionException e) {
            System.out.println("bk-3 refund pay_9: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        assert b1.describe().contains("CANCELLED");
        assert b2.describe().contains("EXPIRED");
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same machine. Frozen dataclasses make each state an immutable value; the base class rejects by default.

# File: state_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import threading
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import List


class IllegalTransitionError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, state: "BookingState", action: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"cannot {action} a booking that is {state.label()}")


class BookingState:
    """Default: reject every operation. Subclasses override only what they allow."""

    def confirm(self, payment_id: str) -> "BookingState":
        raise IllegalTransitionError(self, "confirm")

    def cancel(self) -> "BookingState":
        raise IllegalTransitionError(self, "cancel")

    def expire_if_due(self, now: datetime) -> "BookingState":
        return self

    def label(self) -> str:
        return type(self).__name__.upper()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Held(BookingState):
    hold_until: datetime

    def confirm(self, payment_id: str) -> BookingState:
        return Confirmed(payment_id)

    def cancel(self) -> BookingState:
        return Cancelled("hold released")

    def expire_if_due(self, now: datetime) -> BookingState:
        return self if now < self.hold_until else Expired()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Confirmed(BookingState):
    payment_id: str

    def confirm(self, payment_id: str) -> BookingState:
        if payment_id == self.payment_id:
            return self                                   # idempotent retry
        raise IllegalTransitionError(self, "confirm with a second payment")

    def cancel(self) -> BookingState:
        return Cancelled(f"refund {self.payment_id}")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Expired(BookingState):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Cancelled(BookingState):
    reason: str


class Booking:
    def __init__(self, booking_id: str, now: datetime, hold_for: timedelta) -> None:
        self.id = booking_id
        self._state: BookingState = Held(now + hold_for)
        self._history: List[str] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()                     # transitions are atomic per booking

    def confirm(self, payment_id: str, now: datetime) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._apply(self._state.expire_if_due(now))
            self._apply(self._state.confirm(payment_id))

    def cancel(self, now: datetime) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._apply(self._state.expire_if_due(now))
            self._apply(self._state.cancel())

    def _apply(self, nxt: BookingState) -> None:
        if nxt is not self._state:
            self._history.append(f"{self._state.label()} -> {nxt.label()}")
            self._state = nxt

    def describe(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.id} {self._state} {self._history}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = datetime(2026, 9, 16, 10, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    hold = timedelta(minutes=10)

    b1 = Booking("bk-1", t0, hold)
    b1.confirm("pay_1", t0 + timedelta(minutes=3))
    b1.confirm("pay_1", t0 + timedelta(minutes=3, seconds=5))   # retry: no-op
    b1.cancel(t0 + timedelta(hours=1))
    print(b1.describe())

    b2 = Booking("bk-2", t0, hold)
    try:
        b2.confirm("pay_2", t0 + timedelta(minutes=12))
    except IllegalTransitionError as e:
        print("bk-2 refund pay_2:", e)
    print(b2.describe())

    b3 = Booking("bk-3", t0, hold)
    b3.confirm("pay_3", t0 + timedelta(minutes=1))
    try:
        b3.confirm("pay_9", t0 + timedelta(minutes=1, seconds=30))
    except IllegalTransitionError as e:
        print("bk-3 refund pay_9:", e)

    assert "CANCELLED" in b1.describe()
    assert "EXPIRED" in b2.describe()

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 bk-1 created at 10:00:00Z, hold 10 min → state = Held(holdUntil = 10:10:00Z)
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] confirm("pay_1", 10:03:00)  → expireIfDue: 10:03 < 10:10 → still Held
    │                                → Held.confirm → Confirmed(pay_1)     history: HELD -> CONFIRMED
    ▼
🔁 [2] confirm("pay_1", 10:03:05)  → Confirmed.confirm, same paymentId → returns this → no history entry
    ▼
⚙️ [3] cancel(11:00:00)            → Confirmed.cancel → Cancelled("refund pay_1")
    ▼
🎯 bk-1 Cancelled[reason=refund pay_1] [HELD -> CONFIRMED, CONFIRMED -> CANCELLED]

📥 bk-2 created at 10:00:00Z → Held(holdUntil = 10:10:00Z)
    ▼
⏰ [4] confirm("pay_2", 10:12:00)  → expireIfDue: 10:12 ≥ 10:10 → Expired   history: HELD -> EXPIRED
    ▼
❌ [5] Expired.confirm             → default method → IllegalTransitionException
    │                                "cannot confirm a booking that is EXPIRED" → caller refunds pay_2
    ▼
🎯 bk-2 Expired[] [HELD -> EXPIRED]

📥 bk-3 confirmed with pay_3 at 10:01
    ▼
❌ [6] confirm("pay_9", 10:01:30)  → Confirmed.confirm, different id → "cannot confirm with a second payment a booking that is CONFIRMED"

  1. Step 1 runs expiry before the operation — lazy expiry means correctness doesn't depend on the sweeper having run.

  2. Step 2 is idempotency. Payment providers retry webhooks; treating the retry as an error would page someone for normal behaviour.

  3. Step 4 commits the expiry even though step 5 throws. The booking is genuinely expired; the exception tells the payment handler to refund. Rolling back the expiry would resurrect a hold whose seat may already be resold.

  4. Step 6 is the real conflict — two different payments for one booking — and it's the only confirm-path error that indicates a bug or fraud rather than timing.

9. When TO Use This

  • An entity has a lifecycle and operations are legal only in some stages — booking, order, trip, payment, ticket, elevator, ATM session, vending machine.

  • Behaviour per state is more than allowed/not-allowed — states own data (holdUntil, paymentId) or logic (expiry, idempotency, refund).

  • The follow-up will add states — "now add waitlisted", "now add partially refunded".

  • You see the same switch (status) repeated across several methods. Each method is a column of the same state table; State turns rows into classes.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • Three states, two transitions, no per-state data. An enum and guarded intent methods is shorter and just as safe:

    synchronized void book() {
    if (status != SeatStatus.AVAILABLE) throw new SeatUnavailableException(id);
    status = SeatStatus.BOOKED;
}

  • Transitions are uniform and data-driven — dozens of states configured by operations teams. A transition table (from, event, to) is easier to change and review than dozens of classes.

  • The workflow spans services and days with retries, timers and human approval. Use a workflow engine or a persisted saga, not in-memory state objects.

  • The "states" don't change behaviour, only a label shown in the UI. That's a field.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "State pattern means the state objects must be singletons or stateless."

Reality: Stateless states can be shared, but states that carry data (Held(holdUntil), Confirmed(paymentId)) are ordinary immutable values. Putting that data on the context instead leaves nullable fields that are only meaningful in some states — the bug State is meant to remove.

Misconception: "An invalid transition should be ignored so the system stays up."

Reality: Ignoring confirm on an expired booking keeps the customer's money without a seat. Invalid transitions must be loud — a domain exception the caller handles (refund, retry, alert). The one deliberate exception is an idempotent repeat of a transition that already happened.

Personal misconception (held before learning): TODO — add one you actually held. Not invented here, per the template's no-fabrication rule.

12. Interview Traps

setStatus() as a public method. Any caller can jump from HELD to CONFIRMED without payment. Transitions must be intent methods (→ item 10).

No concurrency story. The follow-up "payment callback and expiry sweeper at the same time" is near-certain in BookMyShow; have the atomic-transition answer ready.

Treating a duplicate payment callback as an error. It's normal provider behaviour; say "idempotent on payment id" before they ask (→ item 32).

Only a sweeper for expiry. If the sweeper lags, expired holds block seats. Mention lazy expiry on access as the correctness mechanism and the sweeper as cleanup (→ item 33).

Drawing a class per state for a trivial machine and not saying why. The judgment call is worth a sentence.

13. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Skipped — no defensible, citable benchmarks for this topic; per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented numbers.

14. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
Latency One virtual call per operation; allocation of a small immutable state on each transition — negligible.
Correctness Illegal transitions fail in one place; the whole graph must still be reviewed across classes.
🧵 Concurrency Each transition is read-decide-write; it must be atomic per aggregate (lock or version CAS).
Extensibility New state = new class, plus edits to the states that transition into it. Not zero-edit.
Visibility The graph is spread across files; keep a diagram (like §5) next to the code.

15. Real World Usage

JDK: java.util.concurrent.FutureTask runs a small internal state machine (NEW → COMPLETING → NORMAL / EXCEPTIONAL / CANCELLED) with CAS transitions — the concurrency half of this note in production code. Thread.State is the enum form.

Spring: Spring Statemachine exists for complex workflows; Spring Batch's BatchStatus models job lifecycle as an enum.

Python: asyncio.Future tracks PENDING / CANCELLED / FINISHED and raises InvalidStateError on an illegal operation — the "throw on invalid transition" rule in the stdlib.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does Command turn into an object? A request: receiver + action + arguments, so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone.
What must an undoable command capture at execute time? The pre-state its inverse needs — e.g., how many items were actually removed.
Why does a new command clear the redo stack? Redo commands were computed against a history that no longer exists.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Command wraps a request as an object — "add two popcorns to cart 42" — instead of calling the method directly. Once it's an object I can put it on a queue, log it, retry it, or undo it. For undo, each command implements execute and undo, and a history keeps two stacks. The subtle part is that undo needs the state as it was at execute time: removing five popcorns from a cart holding two must remember it removed two, or undo creates items out of nothing.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

A Command and a Strategy are both "an object wrapping a function." What's the difference?

A Strategy is how to do something — an interchangeable algorithm the context calls with fresh arguments every time (rule.apply(price, ctx)). A Command is a specific request to do something, with its receiver and arguments already bound (new AddItem(cart, "POPCORN", 2)). You call a strategy many times with different inputs; you execute a command once (and maybe undo it).

That's why Command enables things Strategy doesn't: a command can sit in a queue until a worker picks it up, be serialised to a log and replayed, or be reversed — because it carries everything needed to perform the request.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Undo via inverse commands or via snapshots of state?

Really testing: whether you know inverse operations aren't always available, and what that costs.

Inverse commands (each command knows its own undo) are memory-cheap and work well for invertible, local operations: add/remove, move, rename. Their weakness is fidelity — every command must capture exactly the pre-state it destroys, and some operations have no clean inverse ("apply the best available coupon" depends on the whole cart).

Snapshots (Memento: save the receiver's state before each command) always restore exactly, and commands stay simple, but memory grows with state size × history length. A common hybrid is inverse commands with a periodic snapshot. And for side effects outside your process — an email sent, a card charged — neither works: undo becomes a compensating command (send a correction, issue a refund), which is a different business action, not a reversal.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Command Strategy Memento Domain event
Represents A request to act An algorithm A saved state A fact that happened
Tense Imperative: "add item" — — Past: "item added"
Arguments bound? at creation per call n/a
Undo via undo() via restore (compensate)
Typical LLD use Undo/redo, job queues, elevator requests Pricing, dispatch Editor snapshots Notifications

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Participants: the receiver (Cart) does the real work; commands (AddItem, RemoveItem, ApplyCoupon) bind a receiver to arguments; the invoker (CommandHistory) executes commands and manages the stacks without knowing what any of them do.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — cart undo/redo. Note RemoveItem and ApplyCoupon capture pre-state in execute().

// File: CommandDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

// Receiver: owns the state and the real operations.
final class Cart {
    private final Map<String, Integer> items = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private String coupon;

    void add(String sku, int qty) { items.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); }

    /** Removes up to qty and returns how many were actually removed. */
    int remove(String sku, int qty) {
        int have = items.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
        int removed = Math.min(have, qty);
        if (have - removed == 0) items.remove(sku); else items.put(sku, have - removed);
        return removed;
    }

    String coupon() { return coupon; }
    void useCoupon(String code) { this.coupon = code; }

    @Override public String toString() { return items + (coupon == null ? "" : " coupon=" + coupon); }
}

interface CartCommand {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

record AddItem(Cart cart, String sku, int qty) implements CartCommand {
    public void execute() { cart.add(sku, qty); }
    public void undo() { cart.remove(sku, qty); }
}

final class RemoveItem implements CartCommand {
    private final Cart cart;
    private final String sku;
    private final int requested;
    private int removed;                        // pre-state captured at execute time

    RemoveItem(Cart cart, String sku, int requested) { this.cart = cart; this.sku = sku; this.requested = requested; }

    public void execute() { removed = cart.remove(sku, requested); }
    public void undo() { if (removed > 0) cart.add(sku, removed); }   // restore what was really removed
}

final class ApplyCoupon implements CartCommand {
    private final Cart cart;
    private final String code;
    private String previous;

    ApplyCoupon(Cart cart, String code) { this.cart = cart; this.code = code; }

    public void execute() { previous = cart.coupon(); cart.useCoupon(code); }
    public void undo() { cart.useCoupon(previous); }
}

// Invoker: runs commands, knows nothing about carts.
final class CommandHistory {
    private final Deque<CartCommand> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<CartCommand> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void run(CartCommand command) {
        command.execute();
        undoStack.push(command);
        redoStack.clear();                      // the old future is no longer reachable
    }

    boolean undo() {
        CartCommand command = undoStack.poll();
        if (command == null) return false;
        command.undo();
        redoStack.push(command);
        return true;
    }

    boolean redo() {
        CartCommand command = redoStack.poll();
        if (command == null) return false;
        command.execute();
        undoStack.push(command);
        return true;
    }
}

public class CommandDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        CommandHistory history = new CommandHistory();

        history.run(new AddItem(cart, "POPCORN", 2));
        history.run(new AddItem(cart, "COLA", 1));
        history.run(new RemoveItem(cart, "POPCORN", 5));      // only 2 exist
        history.run(new ApplyCoupon(cart, "FLAT50"));
        System.out.println("after 4 commands : " + cart);

        history.undo();
        history.undo();
        System.out.println("after 2 undos    : " + cart);

        history.redo();
        System.out.println("after 1 redo     : " + cart);

        history.run(new AddItem(cart, "NACHOS", 1));          // clears redo stack
        System.out.println("redo available?  : " + history.redo());
        System.out.println("final            : " + cart);
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same design.

# File: command_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Protocol


class Cart:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._items: Dict[str, int] = {}
        self.coupon: Optional[str] = None

    def add(self, sku: str, qty: int) -> None:
        self._items[sku] = self._items.get(sku, 0) + qty

    def remove(self, sku: str, qty: int) -> int:
        have = self._items.get(sku, 0)
        removed = min(have, qty)
        if have - removed == 0:
            self._items.pop(sku, None)
        else:
            self._items[sku] = have - removed
        return removed

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"{self._items}" + (f" coupon={self.coupon}" if self.coupon else "")


class CartCommand(Protocol):
    def execute(self) -> None: ...
    def undo(self) -> None: ...


class AddItem:
    def __init__(self, cart: Cart, sku: str, qty: int) -> None:
        self.cart, self.sku, self.qty = cart, sku, qty

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self.cart.add(self.sku, self.qty)

    def undo(self) -> None:
        self.cart.remove(self.sku, self.qty)


class RemoveItem:
    def __init__(self, cart: Cart, sku: str, requested: int) -> None:
        self.cart, self.sku, self.requested = cart, sku, requested
        self.removed = 0

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self.removed = self.cart.remove(self.sku, self.requested)   # capture pre-state

    def undo(self) -> None:
        if self.removed:
            self.cart.add(self.sku, self.removed)


class ApplyCoupon:
    def __init__(self, cart: Cart, code: str) -> None:
        self.cart, self.code = cart, code
        self.previous: Optional[str] = None

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self.previous, self.cart.coupon = self.cart.coupon, self.code

    def undo(self) -> None:
        self.cart.coupon = self.previous


class CommandHistory:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._undo: List[CartCommand] = []
        self._redo: List[CartCommand] = []

    def run(self, command: CartCommand) -> None:
        command.execute()
        self._undo.append(command)
        self._redo.clear()

    def undo(self) -> bool:
        if not self._undo:
            return False
        command = self._undo.pop()
        command.undo()
        self._redo.append(command)
        return True

    def redo(self) -> bool:
        if not self._redo:
            return False
        command = self._redo.pop()
        command.execute()
        self._undo.append(command)
        return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cart, history = Cart(), CommandHistory()
    history.run(AddItem(cart, "POPCORN", 2))
    history.run(AddItem(cart, "COLA", 1))
    history.run(RemoveItem(cart, "POPCORN", 5))
    history.run(ApplyCoupon(cart, "FLAT50"))
    print("after 4 commands :", cart)

    history.undo()
    history.undo()
    print("after 2 undos    :", cart)

    history.redo()
    print("after 1 redo     :", cart)

    history.run(AddItem(cart, "NACHOS", 1))
    print("redo available?  :", history.redo())
    print("final            :", cart)

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 empty cart
⚙️ run AddItem(POPCORN,2)      → {POPCORN=2}                         undo=[Add]
⚙️ run AddItem(COLA,1)         → {POPCORN=2, COLA=1}                 undo=[Add,Add]
⚙️ run RemoveItem(POPCORN,5)   → removed=2 captured → {COLA=1}       undo=[..,Remove]
⚙️ run ApplyCoupon(FLAT50)     → previous=null → {COLA=1} coupon=FLAT50
🎯 after 4 commands : {COLA=1} coupon=FLAT50
↩️ undo ApplyCoupon            → coupon=null                          redo=[Coupon]
↩️ undo RemoveItem             → add back removed=2 (not 5) → {COLA=1, POPCORN=2}   redo=[Coupon,Remove]
🎯 after 2 undos    : {COLA=1, POPCORN=2}
↪️ redo RemoveItem             → removed=2 → {COLA=1}                redo=[Coupon]
⚙️ run AddItem(NACHOS,1)       → {COLA=1, NACHOS=1}, redo stack cleared
❌ redo()                      → false

The line that matters is the second undo: restoring 2, the quantity captured at execute time, not the 5 that was requested. An undo that re-adds 5 would silently create three popcorns.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • No queueing, logging, retry or undo requirement. Wrapping every method call in a command class is ceremony; call the method.

  • The operation's effect leaves your process (payment captured, email sent). undo() can't take it back — model a compensating command explicitly instead of pretending it's reversible.

  • Commands need to be durable across restarts. In-memory command objects don't survive a crash; persist them as serialisable job records with an idempotency key.

  • Concurrent edits by multiple users. A per-user undo stack against shared state breaks when another user's change interleaves; that needs operational transforms or CRDTs, not Command.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Undo is just calling the opposite method with the same arguments."

Reality: The opposite method needs the pre-state, which the arguments don't carry. remove(5) on a cart holding 2 removed 2; add(5) is wrong. The command must record what it actually changed during execute().

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • 14-strategy.md — the sibling "behaviour as an object" pattern to distinguish it from.

  • ../02-oo-design-principles/10-encapsulation-of-invariants.md — the receiver keeps its invariants; commands only call its intent methods.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • ../04-concurrency-in-lld/34-background-schedulers.md — scheduled jobs are commands on an executor queue.

  • ../../07-Design-problems/elevator.md — hall and car requests as queued command objects.

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Decorator — intent and structure — Decorator Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Decorator, with the wrapper-stack diagram — Decorator (refactoring.guru)

  • Bonus — the JDK's canonical decorator: BufferedInputStream (Java SE 17 API)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/structural.md.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What problem does it replace? Subclass explosion: n optional add-ons = 2ⁿ subclasses under inheritance, n decorators here.
The structural rule? A decorator implements the same interface it wraps, and delegates to the wrapped object.
Where does wrapping order matter? Any non-commutative step — a percentage fee applied before vs after a flat add-on.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Decorator adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface. A Ticket has a price; Insurance(ticket) is also a Ticket whose price is the inner price plus ₹15, and FoodCombo(Insurance(ticket)) stacks on top. Three optional add-ons are three classes instead of eight subclasses. The same shape is how I add retries or logging to a notifier without touching it. The catch is that wrapping order is semantics — a percentage fee outside a food combo charges on the food too.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why not just subclass Ticket for each add-on?

Because add-ons combine. With insurance, food combo and a convenience fee as independent options, inheritance needs a class for every subset — TicketWithInsurance, TicketWithInsuranceAndFood, and so on, eight classes for three options and sixteen for four. And the combination is fixed at compile time, so a user choosing add-ons at checkout can't be represented without a factory full of conditionals.

Decorators compose at runtime: each add-on is one class, and the checkout builds the stack from the user's selections. The price is more small objects and a deeper call chain when debugging.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

For add-on pricing, would you use nested decorators or a list of pricing rules?

Really testing: whether you pick between two valid designs on concrete grounds instead of by pattern name.

For pricing, a list of PricingRules (→ item 14) is usually cleaner: the order is explicit in one list, rules can be added or removed from config, and there's no object nesting to inspect. The ticket stays a plain value and the engine computes a price from it.

Decorator wins when the add-on changes behaviour of an interface other code already consumes, not just a number — wrapping a Notifier with retries, a PaymentGateway with metrics, an InputStream with buffering. There, callers must keep receiving "a Notifier" and must not know it's decorated. Say both, then pick: pricing → rule list; cross-cutting behaviour on an existing interface → decorator.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Decorator Proxy Adapter Strategy rule list
Interface Same as wrapped Same as wrapped Different from wrapped n/a
Purpose Add behaviour Control access (lazy, remote, auth, cache) Translate an interface Compose a computation
Stacks? by design Usually one Usually one as a list
Who builds it Client, per need Framework / container Integration layer Config / composition root
Example BufferedInputStream Spring @Transactional proxy PaymentGateway over vendor SDK Pricing engine

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Calls travel inward through the wrappers to the base object, and results travel outward, each layer transforming them. The outermost decorator runs its logic last on the way out — which is why the percentage fee, wrapped last, applies to everything inside it.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — priced add-ons, plus behaviour decorators (retry, logging) on a notifier.

// File: DecoratorDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;

// ---------- Priced add-ons ----------
interface Ticket {
    BigDecimal price();
    String description();
}

record BaseTicket(String seat, BigDecimal fare) implements Ticket {
    public BigDecimal price() { return fare; }
    public String description() { return seat; }
}

abstract class TicketAddOn implements Ticket {
    protected final Ticket inner;                  // same interface: decorators stack on decorators
    TicketAddOn(Ticket inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}

final class Insurance extends TicketAddOn {
    Insurance(Ticket inner) { super(inner); }
    public BigDecimal price() { return inner.price().add(new BigDecimal("15.00")); }
    public String description() { return inner.description() + " + insurance"; }
}

final class FoodCombo extends TicketAddOn {
    FoodCombo(Ticket inner) { super(inner); }
    public BigDecimal price() { return inner.price().add(new BigDecimal("180.00")); }
    public String description() { return inner.description() + " + food combo"; }
}

final class ConvenienceFee extends TicketAddOn {
    ConvenienceFee(Ticket inner) { super(inner); }
    public BigDecimal price() {                    // percentage: order-sensitive
        return inner.price().multiply(new BigDecimal("1.02")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
    public String description() { return inner.description() + " + 2% fee"; }
}

// ---------- Behaviour decorators ----------
interface Notifier {
    void send(String userId, String message);
}

final class FlakySmsNotifier implements Notifier {
    private int calls;
    public void send(String userId, String message) {
        if (++calls < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("SMS gateway timeout (attempt " + calls + ")");
        System.out.println("  SMS delivered to " + userId + ": " + message);
    }
}

final class RetryingNotifier implements Notifier {
    private final Notifier inner;
    private final int maxAttempts;
    RetryingNotifier(Notifier inner, int maxAttempts) { this.inner = inner; this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts; }

    public void send(String userId, String message) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                inner.send(userId, message);
                return;
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                if (attempt == maxAttempts) throw e;
                System.out.println("  retrying after: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}

final class LoggingNotifier implements Notifier {
    private final Notifier inner;
    LoggingNotifier(Notifier inner) { this.inner = inner; }

    public void send(String userId, String message) {
        try {
            inner.send(userId, message);
            System.out.println("  [log] send to " + userId + " succeeded");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("  [log] send to " + userId + " failed: " + e.getMessage());
            throw e;                                // log, never swallow
        }
    }
}

public class DecoratorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Ticket ticket = new BaseTicket("GOLD A7", new BigDecimal("350.00"));
        // Built at checkout from the user's selections; the order is deliberate.
        ticket = new ConvenienceFee(new FoodCombo(new Insurance(ticket)));
        System.out.println(ticket.description() + " = " + ticket.price());

        Ticket feeFirst = new FoodCombo(new ConvenienceFee(new Insurance(new BaseTicket("GOLD A7", new BigDecimal("350.00")))));
        System.out.println("fee wrapped inside food = " + feeFirst.price());

        // Callers still see "a Notifier"; retries and logging are invisible to them.
        Notifier notifier = new LoggingNotifier(new RetryingNotifier(new FlakySmsNotifier(), 3));
        notifier.send("u42", "Booking bk-1 confirmed");

        assert ticket.price().equals(new BigDecimal("555.90"));
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — class wrappers for the object-level pattern, and a @retry function decorator to show the related (but different) Python feature.

# File: decorator_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import functools
from decimal import ROUND_HALF_UP, Decimal
from typing import Callable, Protocol


class Ticket(Protocol):
    def price(self) -> Decimal: ...
    def description(self) -> str: ...


class BaseTicket:
    def __init__(self, seat: str, fare: Decimal) -> None:
        self._seat, self._fare = seat, fare

    def price(self) -> Decimal:
        return self._fare

    def description(self) -> str:
        return self._seat


class TicketAddOn:
    def __init__(self, inner: Ticket) -> None:
        self._inner = inner


class Insurance(TicketAddOn):
    def price(self) -> Decimal:
        return self._inner.price() + Decimal("15.00")

    def description(self) -> str:
        return self._inner.description() + " + insurance"


class FoodCombo(TicketAddOn):
    def price(self) -> Decimal:
        return self._inner.price() + Decimal("180.00")

    def description(self) -> str:
        return self._inner.description() + " + food combo"


class ConvenienceFee(TicketAddOn):
    def price(self) -> Decimal:
        return (self._inner.price() * Decimal("1.02")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

    def description(self) -> str:
        return self._inner.description() + " + 2% fee"


# Python's @decorator syntax wraps a FUNCTION; same idea, applied at function level.
def retry(max_attempts: int) -> Callable[[Callable[..., None]], Callable[..., None]]:
    def wrap(fn: Callable[..., None]) -> Callable[..., None]:
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args: object, **kwargs: object) -> None:
            for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except RuntimeError as exc:
                    if attempt == max_attempts:
                        raise
                    print(f"  retrying after: {exc}")
        return wrapper
    return wrap


_calls = {"n": 0}


@retry(max_attempts=3)
def send_sms(user_id: str, message: str) -> None:
    _calls["n"] += 1
    if _calls["n"] < 3:
        raise RuntimeError(f"SMS gateway timeout (attempt {_calls['n']})")
    print(f"  SMS delivered to {user_id}: {message}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ticket: Ticket = ConvenienceFee(FoodCombo(Insurance(BaseTicket("GOLD A7", Decimal("350.00")))))
    print(ticket.description(), "=", ticket.price())

    fee_first = FoodCombo(ConvenienceFee(Insurance(BaseTicket("GOLD A7", Decimal("350.00")))))
    print("fee wrapped inside food =", fee_first.price())

    send_sms("u42", "Booking bk-1 confirmed")
    assert ticket.price() == Decimal("555.90")

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 new ConvenienceFee(new FoodCombo(new Insurance(BaseTicket("GOLD A7", 350.00))))
    │  price() call travels inward ▼, results return outward ▲
    ▼
📦 BaseTicket.price()          → 350.00
⚙️ Insurance.price()           → 350.00 + 15.00  = 365.00
⚙️ FoodCombo.price()           → 365.00 + 180.00 = 545.00
⚙️ ConvenienceFee.price()      → 545.00 × 1.02   = 555.90
🎯 "GOLD A7 + insurance + food combo + 2% fee = 555.90"

🔁 Same add-ons, fee wrapped INSIDE the food combo:
   350.00 → 365.00 → 365.00 × 1.02 = 372.30 → + 180.00 = 552.30   (₹3.60 less)

📥 LoggingNotifier(RetryingNotifier(FlakySms, 3)).send("u42", ...)
   attempt 1 ❌ timeout → retry
   attempt 2 ❌ timeout → retry
   attempt 3 ✅ "SMS delivered to u42" → [log] send to u42 succeeded (logged once, outside the retries)

The ₹3.60 difference is the whole lesson on ordering: whether the convenience fee applies to food is a business rule, and with decorators that rule is encoded in how the object was assembled, which is easy to get wrong at the construction site.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • The add-ons only change a number. A pricing rule list is flatter, puts the order in one visible place, and is easier to drive from config (→ item 14).

  • Callers need to inspect or remove a specific layer ("does this ticket have insurance?"). Decorators hide the stack; that question needs a plain list of selected add-ons on the ticket.

  • Identity or type checks matter. A decorated object is not instanceof BaseTicket, and equals compares wrappers, not the ticket.

  • Only one fixed combination exists. Put the behaviour in the class.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Python's @decorator syntax is the GoF Decorator pattern."

Reality: They share the idea — wrap and delegate — but a Python decorator rewraps a function or class definition at definition time, while GoF Decorator wraps an object instance at runtime behind a shared interface. @retry on send_sms affects every call forever; RetryingNotifier(notifier) can be applied to one instance and not another.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • ../02-oo-design-principles/08-composition-over-inheritance.md — Decorator is composition solving the subclass-explosion problem.

  • ../05-modeling-craft/37-never-use-double-for-money.md — every price in the stack is BigDecimal.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • 24-adapter-and-facade.md — the other wrapper pattern; same shape, different interface.

  • 23-chain-of-responsibility.md — a chain of wrappers where each may short-circuit is a filter chain.
