headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Builder — intent and structure — Builder Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Builder, with the director variant — Builder (refactoring.guru)

  • Python's native alternative (keyword args + frozen dataclasses) — dataclasses — Python docs

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/creational.md.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
When does a constructor need a builder? >~4 params, several optional, or adjacent params of the same type (silent transposition).
Where do required fields go? In the builder's entry method (builder(showId, userId)), so forgetting one won't compile.
Where does validation happen? In build(), across fields — then return an immutable object.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Builder constructs an object with many optional fields step by step and hands back an immutable, validated instance. A booking request has required show and user, then optional seats, coupon, insurance and payment method. A twelve-argument constructor invites passing userId where showId goes — both are strings, so it compiles. With a builder every value is named, required fields are enforced by the entry method, and build() validates cross-field rules once. In Python, keyword arguments on a frozen dataclass usually make a builder unnecessary.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does a builder give you over a constructor with named local variables at the call site?

Three things the call site can't. Names at the point of use: new BookingRequest("s-42", "u-7", ...) doesn't tell a reader which string is which, and swapping them compiles. Optional fields without telescoping constructors: no BookingRequest(show, user), BookingRequest(show, user, coupon), BookingRequest(show, user, coupon, insurance) ladder. One validation point: rules that span fields ("insurance requires at least one seat", "max 10 seats") run in build(), so an invalid object can't exist.

The fourth, less obvious benefit is immutability: the builder is the mutable scratchpad, and the product can have all-final fields with defensive copies of collections.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Builder, a Java record, or a static factory — how do you choose for a new class?

Really testing: whether you'd write a builder for a three-field class.

A record with a compact constructor is the right default for small value objects: record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) — two or three required fields, all meaningful, validation in the compact constructor. A static factory method earns its place when construction has a meaningful name or can return cached/subtype instances (Money.zero(INR)).

A builder is justified when optional fields accumulate, or when there are several parameters of the same type in a row. The cost is real — a second class, duplicated field declarations, and a builder that can drift out of sync when a field is added. For fewer than about four fields, typed value objects (ShowId, UserId) solve the transposition problem more cheaply than a builder (→ item 36).

4. Quick Comparison Table

Telescoping constructors JavaBean setters Builder Record / dataclass
Named arguments Java · Python kwargs
Immutable result
Valid at all times half-built objects exist
Many optional fields explosion Java: no defaults
Boilerplate Medium Low High Lowest

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

The builder is the only mutable object in the flow, and it never escapes into the domain. toBuilder() is how you "modify" an immutable product: copy into a new builder, change, build a new instance.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — a booking request with required fields enforced by the entry method, validation in build(), and toBuilder().

// File: BuilderDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;

enum PaymentMethod { UPI, CARD, WALLET }

final class BookingRequest {
    private static final int MAX_SEATS = 10;

    private final String showId;
    private final String userId;
    private final List<String> seats;
    private final String couponCode;        // null = none
    private final boolean insurance;
    private final PaymentMethod paymentMethod;

    private BookingRequest(Builder b) {      // only the builder can call this
        this.showId = b.showId;
        this.userId = b.userId;
        this.seats = List.copyOf(b.seats);   // defensive, unmodifiable copy
        this.couponCode = b.couponCode;
        this.insurance = b.insurance;
        this.paymentMethod = b.paymentMethod;
    }

    /** Required fields here: forgetting one is a compile error, not a runtime one. */
    static Builder builder(String showId, String userId) { return new Builder(showId, userId); }

    Builder toBuilder() {
        Builder b = new Builder(showId, userId);
        b.seats.addAll(seats);
        b.couponCode = couponCode;
        b.insurance = insurance;
        b.paymentMethod = paymentMethod;
        return b;
    }

    List<String> seats() { return seats; }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return "BookingRequest{show=" + showId + ", user=" + userId + ", seats=" + seats
                + ", coupon=" + couponCode + ", insurance=" + insurance + ", pay=" + paymentMethod + "}";
    }

    static final class Builder {
        private final String showId;
        private final String userId;
        private final List<String> seats = new ArrayList<>();
        private String couponCode;
        private boolean insurance;
        private PaymentMethod paymentMethod = PaymentMethod.UPI;   // sensible default

        private Builder(String showId, String userId) {
            if (showId == null || userId == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("showId and userId are required");
            this.showId = showId;
            this.userId = userId;
        }

        Builder seat(String seatId) { seats.add(seatId); return this; }
        Builder coupon(String code) { this.couponCode = code; return this; }
        Builder withInsurance() { this.insurance = true; return this; }
        Builder paymentMethod(PaymentMethod method) { this.paymentMethod = method; return this; }

        BookingRequest build() {
            // Cross-field rules live in exactly one place.
            if (seats.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("at least one seat is required");
            if (seats.size() > MAX_SEATS) throw new IllegalStateException("max " + MAX_SEATS + " seats per booking");
            if (new HashSet<>(seats).size() != seats.size()) throw new IllegalStateException("duplicate seat in " + seats);
            if (couponCode != null && !couponCode.matches("[A-Z0-9]{4,12}")) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("malformed coupon: " + couponCode);
            }
            return new BookingRequest(this);
        }
    }
}

public class BuilderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BookingRequest request = BookingRequest.builder("show-42", "user-7")
                .seat("A7").seat("A8")
                .coupon("FLAT50")
                .withInsurance()
                .build();
        System.out.println(request);

        try {
            BookingRequest.builder("show-42", "user-7").seat("A7").seat("A7").build();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        BookingRequest card = request.toBuilder().paymentMethod(PaymentMethod.CARD).coupon(null).build();
        System.out.println(card);
        System.out.println("original unchanged: " + request);

        try {
            request.seats().add("Z1");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("seats list is immutable");
        }
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — the idiomatic version is a frozen dataclass: keyword arguments give names and defaults, __post_init__ validates, dataclasses.replace is toBuilder(). A fluent builder is shown after it for parity — use it only when construction is genuinely stepwise.

# File: builder_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import dataclasses
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


class PaymentMethod(Enum):
    UPI = "UPI"
    CARD = "CARD"
    WALLET = "WALLET"


MAX_SEATS = 10


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BookingRequest:
    show_id: str
    user_id: str
    seats: Tuple[str, ...]                        # tuple: immutable
    coupon_code: Optional[str] = None
    insurance: bool = False
    payment_method: PaymentMethod = PaymentMethod.UPI

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:              # the build() validation, run on every construction
        if not self.seats:
            raise ValueError("at least one seat is required")
        if len(self.seats) > MAX_SEATS:
            raise ValueError(f"max {MAX_SEATS} seats per booking")
        if len(set(self.seats)) != len(self.seats):
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate seat in {list(self.seats)}")
        if self.coupon_code is not None and not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z0-9]{4,12}", self.coupon_code):
            raise ValueError(f"malformed coupon: {self.coupon_code}")


class BookingRequestBuilder:
    """Only worth it when values arrive over several steps (e.g., a multi-page checkout)."""

    def __init__(self, show_id: str, user_id: str) -> None:
        self._show_id, self._user_id = show_id, user_id
        self._seats: List[str] = []
        self._coupon: Optional[str] = None
        self._insurance = False

    def seat(self, seat_id: str) -> "BookingRequestBuilder":
        self._seats.append(seat_id)
        return self

    def coupon(self, code: str) -> "BookingRequestBuilder":
        self._coupon = code
        return self

    def with_insurance(self) -> "BookingRequestBuilder":
        self._insurance = True
        return self

    def build(self) -> BookingRequest:
        return BookingRequest(self._show_id, self._user_id, tuple(self._seats), self._coupon, self._insurance)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    request = BookingRequest("show-42", "user-7", ("A7", "A8"), coupon_code="FLAT50", insurance=True)
    print(request)

    try:
        BookingRequest("show-42", "user-7", ("A7", "A7"))
    except ValueError as e:
        print("rejected:", e)

    card = dataclasses.replace(request, payment_method=PaymentMethod.CARD, coupon_code=None)
    print(card)
    print("original unchanged:", request)

    stepwise = BookingRequestBuilder("show-42", "user-7").seat("B1").with_insurance().build()
    print(stepwise)

    try:
        request.seats = ("Z1",)  # type: ignore[misc]
    except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
        print("BookingRequest is immutable")

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 builder("show-42", "user-7")                  → required fields checked non-null
⚙️ .seat("A7").seat("A8")                         → seats = [A7, A8]
⚙️ .coupon("FLAT50").withInsurance()              → coupon = FLAT50, insurance = true, pay = UPI (default)
🤔 .build()                                       → 2 seats ≤ 10 ✅ · no duplicates ✅ · coupon matches [A-Z0-9]{4,12} ✅
✅ BookingRequest{show=show-42, user=user-7, seats=[A7, A8], coupon=FLAT50, insurance=true, pay=UPI}

📥 builder(...).seat("A7").seat("A7").build()
❌ duplicate check                                → "duplicate seat in [A7, A7]" — no object exists

📥 request.toBuilder().paymentMethod(CARD).coupon(null).build()
✅ new instance with pay=CARD, coupon=null        → original still pay=UPI, coupon=FLAT50

📥 request.seats().add("Z1")
❌ UnsupportedOperationException                  → List.copyOf made the field unmodifiable

The duplicate-seat rejection is the design argument: validation that spans fields runs once, before the object exists, so no downstream code needs to re-check seats for duplicates.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • Three or fewer fields, all required. A record or plain constructor is shorter; the builder is ceremony (→ item 26).

  • Python or Kotlin with keyword arguments and defaults. The language already provides names, defaults and immutability; a builder adds nothing but code.

  • The object is a mutable entity with a lifecycle. Builders produce values; an entity is created once and then changes through intent methods (→ item 10).

  • Fields are frequently added. Every new field must be added in three places (field, builder field, builder method) — without code generation, the builder drifts.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Builder is for making object creation fluent."

Reality: Fluency is a side effect. The point is that the product is never observable in an invalid or half-initialised state, and can be immutable. A fluent API that returns a mutable object with setters has kept the syntax and lost the guarantee.

  • 26-pattern-overuse.md — a builder on a three-field record is a standard overuse example.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What's fixed and what varies? The step order is fixed in a final base method; individual steps vary in subclasses.
Abstract step vs hook? Abstract: subclass must implement. Hook: has a default, subclass may override.
Its main weakness? It's inheritance: two independently varying steps means a subclass per combination.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton in a base class and lets subclasses fill in specific steps. A payment flow is always validate, authorise, capture, notify — that order lives in a final process() method. Card and UPI subclasses implement authorize and capture differently, and a hook like requiresStepUpAuth lets card payments add an OTP above a threshold. It guarantees nobody skips validation. The cost is inheritance: once two steps vary independently, I switch to injecting a strategy per step.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why is the template method final, and what's a hook?

final is what makes it a template: the base class guarantees the invariant sequence — validate before authorise, capture only after authorise, always notify. Without final, a subclass can override process() and skip validation, and the pattern's only guarantee is gone.

A hook is a step with a do-nothing or default implementation that subclasses may override to extend the flow at a predefined point — requiresStepUpAuth() returns false by default and card payments override it. Abstract steps are mandatory variation; hooks are optional extension. A base class with ten hooks is a sign the skeleton isn't really fixed.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Template Method or Strategy-per-step for the payment flow?

Really testing: whether you recognise the moment inheritance stops scaling.

Template Method is the lighter choice when exactly one axis varies — the payment instrument — and each subclass changes one or two steps. The code reads top to bottom and the skeleton is enforced by the compiler.

It breaks when steps vary independently. If authorisation varies by instrument (card, UPI, wallet) and step-up authentication varies by risk policy (none, OTP, biometric), inheritance needs nine subclasses. Composition needs three Authorizers and three StepUpPolicys injected into one PaymentFlow — the skeleton is still fixed in one non-overridable method, but each step is a strategy (→ item 14). Say the number: one varying axis → Template Method; two or more → strategies.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Template Method Strategy per step
Mechanism Inheritance: subclass overrides steps Composition: steps injected
Skeleton enforced by final method in base class The one flow class that calls the steps
Varying axes supported One, cleanly Many, independently
Change at runtime fixed per subclass swap a step
Class count, 3 × 3 variants 9 subclasses 6 small classes
Testability Test through the subclass Test each step alone

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Green steps belong to the base class and run identically for every payment type; amber steps are the subclass's; the purple diamond is a hook. The "Hollywood principle" describes the control flow: the base class calls the subclass, never the reverse.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — a payment flow with a final skeleton, two abstract steps and one hook.

// File: TemplateMethodDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

record PaymentRequest(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {}

record PaymentResult(String orderId, String captureId, List<String> steps) {}

abstract class PaymentFlow {
    private static final BigDecimal ZERO = BigDecimal.ZERO;

    /** The template method. final: no subclass can skip validation or reorder capture before auth. */
    public final PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
        List<String> steps = new ArrayList<>();
        validate(request, steps);
        if (requiresStepUpAuth(request)) {            // hook
            steps.add("step-up auth (OTP) passed");
        }
        String authId = authorize(request);           // varies
        steps.add("authorized " + authId);
        String captureId = capture(request, authId);  // varies
        steps.add("captured " + captureId);
        steps.add("notified user for " + request.orderId());
        return new PaymentResult(request.orderId(), captureId, steps);
    }

    private void validate(PaymentRequest request, List<String> steps) {
        if (request.amount().compareTo(ZERO) <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive: " + request.amount());
        }
        steps.add("validated " + request.amount());
    }

    /** Hook with a safe default. Subclasses MAY override. */
    protected boolean requiresStepUpAuth(PaymentRequest request) { return false; }

    /** Abstract steps. Subclasses MUST implement. */
    protected abstract String authorize(PaymentRequest request);
    protected abstract String capture(PaymentRequest request, String authId);
}

final class CardPaymentFlow extends PaymentFlow {
    private static final BigDecimal OTP_THRESHOLD = new BigDecimal("2000.00");

    @Override
    protected boolean requiresStepUpAuth(PaymentRequest request) {
        return request.amount().compareTo(OTP_THRESHOLD) > 0;
    }

    @Override
    protected String authorize(PaymentRequest request) { return "card-auth-" + request.orderId(); }

    @Override
    protected String capture(PaymentRequest request, String authId) { return "card-cap-" + request.orderId(); }
}

final class UpiPaymentFlow extends PaymentFlow {
    @Override
    protected String authorize(PaymentRequest request) { return "upi-collect-" + request.orderId(); }

    @Override
    protected String capture(PaymentRequest request, String authId) { return "upi-settled-" + request.orderId(); }
}

public class TemplateMethodDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentFlow card = new CardPaymentFlow();
        PaymentFlow upi = new UpiPaymentFlow();

        System.out.println(card.process(new PaymentRequest("o-1", new BigDecimal("2500.00"))).steps());
        System.out.println(card.process(new PaymentRequest("o-2", new BigDecimal("370.00"))).steps());
        System.out.println(upi.process(new PaymentRequest("o-3", new BigDecimal("370.00"))).steps());

        try {
            upi.process(new PaymentRequest("o-4", new BigDecimal("0.00")));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected before any provider call: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same skeleton with abc. Python can't enforce final at runtime; typing.final documents intent for type checkers.

# File: template_method_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import List, final


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaymentRequest:
    order_id: str
    amount: Decimal


class PaymentFlow(ABC):
    @final                                           # enforced by mypy/pyright, not at runtime
    def process(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> List[str]:
        steps: List[str] = []
        self._validate(request, steps)
        if self.requires_step_up_auth(request):      # hook
            steps.append("step-up auth (OTP) passed")
        auth_id = self.authorize(request)
        steps.append(f"authorized {auth_id}")
        capture_id = self.capture(request, auth_id)
        steps.append(f"captured {capture_id}")
        steps.append(f"notified user for {request.order_id}")
        return steps

    def _validate(self, request: PaymentRequest, steps: List[str]) -> None:
        if request.amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"amount must be positive: {request.amount}")
        steps.append(f"validated {request.amount}")

    def requires_step_up_auth(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> bool:
        return False                                  # default hook

    @abstractmethod
    def authorize(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> str: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def capture(self, request: PaymentRequest, auth_id: str) -> str: ...


class CardPaymentFlow(PaymentFlow):
    OTP_THRESHOLD = Decimal("2000.00")

    def requires_step_up_auth(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> bool:
        return request.amount > self.OTP_THRESHOLD

    def authorize(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> str:
        return f"card-auth-{request.order_id}"

    def capture(self, request: PaymentRequest, auth_id: str) -> str:
        return f"card-cap-{request.order_id}"


class UpiPaymentFlow(PaymentFlow):
    def authorize(self, request: PaymentRequest) -> str:
        return f"upi-collect-{request.order_id}"

    def capture(self, request: PaymentRequest, auth_id: str) -> str:
        return f"upi-settled-{request.order_id}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    card, upi = CardPaymentFlow(), UpiPaymentFlow()
    print(card.process(PaymentRequest("o-1", Decimal("2500.00"))))
    print(card.process(PaymentRequest("o-2", Decimal("370.00"))))
    print(upi.process(PaymentRequest("o-3", Decimal("370.00"))))
    try:
        upi.process(PaymentRequest("o-4", Decimal("0.00")))
    except ValueError as e:
        print("rejected before any provider call:", e)

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 CardPaymentFlow.process(o-1, 2500.00)
⚙️ validate               → 2500.00 > 0 ✅
🤔 hook (Card override)   → 2500.00 > 2000.00 → true → "step-up auth (OTP) passed"
🧮 authorize (Card)       → "card-auth-o-1"
🧮 capture (Card)         → "card-cap-o-1"
⚙️ notifyUser             → "notified user for o-1"

📥 CardPaymentFlow.process(o-2, 370.00)
🤔 hook                   → 370.00 ≤ 2000.00 → false → no OTP step

📥 UpiPaymentFlow.process(o-3, 370.00)
🤔 hook (default)         → false
🧮 authorize / capture    → "upi-collect-o-3" / "upi-settled-o-3"

📥 UpiPaymentFlow.process(o-4, 0.00)
❌ validate (base class)  → "amount must be positive: 0.00" — neither subclass step ran

The last trace is the pattern's guarantee: the rejection happened in the base class before any subclass code ran, and no subclass can override process() to skip it.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • More than one step varies independently. Subclass count multiplies; inject a strategy per step instead:

    final class PaymentFlow {
    private final Authorizer authorizer;       // CardAuthorizer, UpiAuthorizer, ...
    private final StepUpPolicy stepUp;          // NoStepUp, OtpAbove(2000), ...
    PaymentFlow(Authorizer a, StepUpPolicy s) { this.authorizer = a; this.stepUp = s; }
}

  • The variant must change at runtime (switch provider on failure). A subclass is fixed at construction; a strategy can be swapped.

  • The base class keeps growing hooks. If every new requirement adds a hook, the "fixed skeleton" isn't fixed — it's a framework in disguise.

  • Subclasses need to call steps in a different order. Then there is no common skeleton; don't force one.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Template Method and Strategy solve different problems."

Reality: They solve the same problem — vary part of an algorithm — with different mechanisms. Template Method uses inheritance and varies steps at compile time; Strategy uses composition and varies whole algorithms (or steps) at runtime. Choosing between them is the interview question.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • ../02-oo-design-principles/08-composition-over-inheritance.md — the reason Template Method gives way to strategies.

  • 14-strategy.md — the composition-based alternative.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • 24-adapter-and-facade.md — provider-specific authorize/capture steps are usually adapters over vendor SDKs.

  • 23-chain-of-responsibility.md — when the "steps" become a variable-length pipeline.

Reference Links

  • Bonus — a stdlib chain: handler propagation in logging — Python docs

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one design question to answer out loud? Does a handler stop the chain, or does every handler run (pass-through)?
How to order a validation chain? Security first, then cheapest-to-evaluate, then expensive lookups last.
Linked next pointers or a list? A list pipeline is easier to configure and test; linked is the textbook form.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Chain of Responsibility passes a request through an ordered series of handlers, each of which can handle it, reject it, or pass it on. Booking validation is a chain: authenticate, rate-limit, check seat count, check availability — the first rejection stops it. Adding a fraud check is a new handler inserted at a position, with no edit to the others. The question I'd answer explicitly is stop versus pass-through: validation stops at the first failure, but a discount chain usually lets every eligible discount apply unless one is exclusive.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Classic linked handlers with next, or a list of handlers run by a pipeline?

The GoF form links each handler to the next, and each handler decides whether to call next. It's flexible — a handler can do work after the rest of the chain returns, which is how servlet filters and middleware time a request — but the chain's shape is spread across every handler's wiring, and forgetting to call next silently truncates it.

A list pipeline keeps the order in one place (List.of(auth, rateLimit, seatLimit, availability)), makes reordering a config change, and centralises the stop rule. For validation and discounts in LLD, the list is usually clearer. Use linked handlers when a handler must wrap the rest of the chain (before-and-after logic), which is the middleware case.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Coupon stacking: should a discount handler stop the chain or pass through?

Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up once a discount or coupon chain appears in e-commerce and booking designs.

Really testing: whether you treat stop semantics and order as business rules, not implementation details.

Pass-through is the default for stackable discounts — member 5%, festival ₹20 — every eligible handler adjusts the price and the order determines the result, just like composable pricing rules (→ item 14). Stop semantics are needed for exclusivity: a VIP coupon that "cannot be combined with other offers" must end the chain after applying.

So the handler's return value needs to carry both the new price and a stop flag, and the exclusive handler must run first, or the stackable ones have already applied by the time it says stop. Put the order and the exclusivity rule in a test with named cases — this is where revenue bugs come from.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Chain of Responsibility Decorator Strategy rule list Observer
Can short-circuit core feature possible, unusual usually all run all listeners run
Handlers know each other Linked form: next only Wraps one inner No No
Result Handled / rejected / transformed Same interface, enriched Folded value None (side effects)
Order matters Should not
LLD use Validation, filters, approvals Retry/logging wrappers Pricing Notifications

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Ordering rule: reject unauthenticated traffic before spending anything on it, then apply cheap in-memory checks, and put the handler that reads shared state (seat availability) last — so the most expensive check only runs for requests that passed everything else.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — a short-circuiting validation chain (linked form) and a pass-through discount pipeline with an exclusive handler (list form).

// File: ChainDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.Set;

record BookingAttempt(String userId, String authToken, int requestsThisMinute, List<String> seats) {}

record Rejection(String handler, String reason) {}

// ---------- 1. Short-circuit chain, linked form ----------
abstract class BookingHandler {
    private BookingHandler next;

    /** Returns the argument so chains read left to right: a.linkWith(b).linkWith(c). */
    BookingHandler linkWith(BookingHandler next) { this.next = next; return next; }

    final Optional<Rejection> handle(BookingAttempt attempt) {
        Optional<Rejection> rejection = check(attempt);
        if (rejection.isPresent() || next == null) return rejection;   // first rejection stops the chain
        return next.handle(attempt);
    }

    protected abstract Optional<Rejection> check(BookingAttempt attempt);

    protected Optional<Rejection> reject(String reason) {
        return Optional.of(new Rejection(getClass().getSimpleName(), reason));
    }
}

final class AuthHandler extends BookingHandler {
    protected Optional<Rejection> check(BookingAttempt a) {
        // Stand-in for real token verification.
        return a.authToken().equals("tok-" + a.userId()) ? Optional.empty() : reject("invalid token");
    }
}

final class RateLimitHandler extends BookingHandler {
    protected Optional<Rejection> check(BookingAttempt a) {
        return a.requestsThisMinute() <= 5 ? Optional.empty() : reject("rate limit exceeded");
    }
}

final class SeatLimitHandler extends BookingHandler {
    protected Optional<Rejection> check(BookingAttempt a) {
        return a.seats().size() <= 10 ? Optional.empty() : reject("more than 10 seats");
    }
}

final class AvailabilityHandler extends BookingHandler {
    private final Set<String> bookedSeats;
    AvailabilityHandler(Set<String> bookedSeats) { this.bookedSeats = Set.copyOf(bookedSeats); }

    protected Optional<Rejection> check(BookingAttempt a) {
        return a.seats().stream().filter(bookedSeats::contains).findFirst()
                .map(seat -> new Rejection("AvailabilityHandler", "seat " + seat + " already booked"));
    }
}

// ---------- 2. Pass-through pipeline with an exclusive stop, list form ----------
record DiscountStep(BigDecimal price, boolean stop) {}

@FunctionalInterface
interface DiscountHandler {
    DiscountStep apply(BigDecimal price, String coupon);
}

final class DiscountPipeline {
    private final List<DiscountHandler> handlers;   // order lives here, in one place
    DiscountPipeline(List<DiscountHandler> handlers) { this.handlers = List.copyOf(handlers); }

    BigDecimal run(BigDecimal price, String coupon) {
        for (DiscountHandler handler : handlers) {
            DiscountStep step = handler.apply(price, coupon);
            price = step.price();
            if (step.stop()) break;
        }
        return price.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
}

public class ChainDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BookingHandler chain = new AuthHandler();
        chain.linkWith(new RateLimitHandler())
             .linkWith(new SeatLimitHandler())
             .linkWith(new AvailabilityHandler(Set.of("A7")));

        List<BookingAttempt> attempts = List.of(
                new BookingAttempt("u1", "tok-u1", 1, List.of("B1", "B2")),
                new BookingAttempt("u2", "forged", 1, List.of("B3")),
                new BookingAttempt("u3", "tok-u3", 9, List.of("B4")),
                new BookingAttempt("u4", "tok-u4", 2, List.of("A7", "A8")));
        for (BookingAttempt attempt : attempts) {
            System.out.println(attempt.userId() + " -> " + chain.handle(attempt).map(Rejection::toString).orElse("ACCEPTED"));
        }

        DiscountHandler exclusiveVip = (p, c) -> "VIP100".equals(c)
                ? new DiscountStep(p.subtract(new BigDecimal("100")), true)   // cannot combine: stop
                : new DiscountStep(p, false);
        DiscountHandler member = (p, c) -> new DiscountStep(p.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.95")), false);
        DiscountHandler festival = (p, c) -> new DiscountStep(p.subtract(new BigDecimal("20")), false);

        DiscountPipeline discounts = new DiscountPipeline(List.of(exclusiveVip, member, festival));
        System.out.println("no coupon : " + discounts.run(new BigDecimal("370.00"), null));
        System.out.println("VIP100    : " + discounts.run(new BigDecimal("370.00"), "VIP100"));
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same two chains; the linked form uses a base class, the pipeline uses plain callables.

# File: chain_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import ROUND_HALF_UP, Decimal
from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, List, NamedTuple, Optional, Sequence


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BookingAttempt:
    user_id: str
    auth_token: str
    requests_this_minute: int
    seats: Sequence[str]


class Rejection(NamedTuple):
    handler: str
    reason: str


class BookingHandler:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._next: Optional[BookingHandler] = None

    def link_with(self, nxt: "BookingHandler") -> "BookingHandler":
        self._next = nxt
        return nxt

    def handle(self, attempt: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        rejection = self.check(attempt)
        if rejection is not None or self._next is None:
            return rejection
        return self._next.handle(attempt)

    def check(self, attempt: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def reject(self, reason: str) -> Rejection:
        return Rejection(type(self).__name__, reason)


class AuthHandler(BookingHandler):
    def check(self, a: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        return None if a.auth_token == f"tok-{a.user_id}" else self.reject("invalid token")


class RateLimitHandler(BookingHandler):
    def check(self, a: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        return None if a.requests_this_minute <= 5 else self.reject("rate limit exceeded")


class SeatLimitHandler(BookingHandler):
    def check(self, a: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        return None if len(a.seats) <= 10 else self.reject("more than 10 seats")


class AvailabilityHandler(BookingHandler):
    def __init__(self, booked: FrozenSet[str]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._booked = booked

    def check(self, a: BookingAttempt) -> Optional[Rejection]:
        taken = next((s for s in a.seats if s in self._booked), None)
        return None if taken is None else self.reject(f"seat {taken} already booked")


class DiscountStep(NamedTuple):
    price: Decimal
    stop: bool


DiscountHandler = Callable[[Decimal, Optional[str]], DiscountStep]


def run_discounts(handlers: List[DiscountHandler], price: Decimal, coupon: Optional[str]) -> Decimal:
    for handler in handlers:
        price, stop = handler(price, coupon)
        if stop:
            break
    return price.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    chain = AuthHandler()
    chain.link_with(RateLimitHandler()).link_with(SeatLimitHandler()).link_with(AvailabilityHandler(frozenset({"A7"})))

    for attempt in [
        BookingAttempt("u1", "tok-u1", 1, ["B1", "B2"]),
        BookingAttempt("u2", "forged", 1, ["B3"]),
        BookingAttempt("u3", "tok-u3", 9, ["B4"]),
        BookingAttempt("u4", "tok-u4", 2, ["A7", "A8"]),
    ]:
        print(attempt.user_id, "->", chain.handle(attempt) or "ACCEPTED")

    def exclusive_vip(p: Decimal, c: Optional[str]) -> DiscountStep:
        return DiscountStep(p - Decimal("100"), True) if c == "VIP100" else DiscountStep(p, False)

    def member(p: Decimal, c: Optional[str]) -> DiscountStep:
        return DiscountStep(p * Decimal("0.95"), False)

    def festival(p: Decimal, c: Optional[str]) -> DiscountStep:
        return DiscountStep(p - Decimal("20"), False)

    handlers = [exclusive_vip, member, festival]
    print("no coupon :", run_discounts(handlers, Decimal("370.00"), None))
    print("VIP100    :", run_discounts(handlers, Decimal("370.00"), "VIP100"))

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 u1 (tok-u1, 1 req/min, [B1,B2])  → Auth ✅ → RateLimit ✅ → SeatLimit ✅ → Availability ✅ → ACCEPTED
📥 u2 (forged token)                 → Auth ❌ "invalid token"            (3 handlers never ran)
📥 u3 (9 req/min)                    → Auth ✅ → RateLimit ❌ "rate limit exceeded"
📥 u4 ([A7,A8], A7 booked)           → Auth ✅ → RateLimit ✅ → SeatLimit ✅ → Availability ❌ "seat A7 already booked"

📥 discounts on 370.00, no coupon
   exclusiveVip → not VIP100 → 370.00, continue
   member       → 370.00 × 0.95 = 351.50, continue
   festival     → 351.50 − 20   = 331.50, continue
🎯 331.50

📥 discounts on 370.00, coupon VIP100
   exclusiveVip → 370.00 − 100 = 270.00, STOP
🎯 270.00   (member and festival never ran — "cannot be combined")

The u2 line shows why auth goes first: a forged request never reaches the availability check, which in production is the handler that reads shared state. The VIP line shows why the exclusive handler must be first — placed last, member and festival would already have applied.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • Every step always runs and none can stop the flow. That's a plain sequence of calls or a strategy rule list; a chain adds wiring for nothing.

  • Exactly one handler should process each request, chosen by type. A map from type to handler (a registry, → item 15) is O(1) and explicit; walking a chain to find the owner is slower and hides the routing.

  • Handlers need each other's results in complex ways. When step 4 depends on data computed in steps 2 and 3, a chain with a shared mutable context turns into implicit coupling — model the workflow explicitly.

  • The chain is long and a request "falls off the end" unhandled. Always define what happens when no handler takes responsibility; silence is the classic bug.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "In Chain of Responsibility exactly one handler handles the request."

Reality: That's the original GoF framing, but the pattern as used in practice (servlet filters, middleware, validation pipelines, discount chains) often lets several handlers act. What defines it is the ordered, decoupled sequence with the option to stop — so state the stop semantics every time.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • ../05-modeling-craft/40-custom-exceptions-for-domain-failures.md — rejections as typed results or domain exceptions.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • 20-decorator.md — middleware that wraps the rest of the chain is a decorator stack.

  • ../../07-Design-problems/high-concurrency-flash-sale-system.md — request filtering in front of a contended resource.

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Adapter — Adapter Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Facade — Facade Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

  • Adapter, with object vs class adapter — Adapter (refactoring.guru)

  • Bonus — Facade (refactoring.guru)

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/structural.md.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Adapter vs Facade in one line each? Adapter: make X look like the interface I own. Facade: one simple entry to a complex subsystem.
"Support three payment providers" — the answer? One PaymentGateway interface we own; one adapter per provider SDK.
A provider call times out. Failed? No — unknown. Map to PENDING and reconcile; never release the seat or retry blindly.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Adapter and Facade are both boundary patterns. An adapter makes a class I can't change — a vendor SDK — implement an interface I own. For three payment providers I define PaymentGateway in domain terms and write one adapter per SDK, which converts amounts, maps status codes and translates exceptions. A facade is different: it gives callers one simple method, like checkout(), over several subsystems — inventory, payment, notification. The real work in the adapter is keeping vendor concepts from leaking in, especially mapping a timeout to "unknown", not "failed".

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy all wrap something. How do you tell them apart?

By what happens to the interface. An adapter changes it — the SDK's createCharge(long cents, ...) becomes our charge(orderId, BigDecimal). A facade simplifies it — many subsystem interfaces collapse into one coarse-grained method. A decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour; a proxy keeps the same interface and controls access.

In LLD you are almost always writing an adapter at the third-party boundary and occasionally a facade as the application-service entry point. If a candidate calls a class with a different interface a "decorator," that's the tell that they're matching on "wrapper" rather than on intent.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

What belongs inside the adapter, and what must never cross it?

Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up to "how do you support multiple payment providers?"

Really testing: whether you design the port in domain terms or just re-export the first vendor's API.

Inside the adapter: unit conversion (rupees ↔ minor units, decimal strings), status mapping into our enum, exception translation into our result or exception types, idempotency-key plumbing, and vendor-specific retries. What must not cross: vendor enums (requires_action), vendor exception classes, vendor IDs used as our primary keys, and vendor-only fields sprinkled into shared models. If CheckoutService ever says if (status.equals("requires_action")), the fourth provider will need edits in shared code — which is exactly what the pattern was supposed to prevent.

The design trap is shaping the interface after the first provider. Define PaymentGateway by what checkout needs (charge, refund, status query → SUCCEEDED / PENDING / FAILED) and make every provider fit it — including mapping timeouts to PENDING, because a network timeout after the request was sent means the charge may have happened.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Adapter Facade Decorator Proxy
Interface Converts to a different one New, simpler one over many Same as wrapped Same as wrapped
Wraps One incompatible class A whole subsystem One object One object
Intent Compatibility Simplicity / layering Add behaviour Control access
LLD instance AcmePayAdapter implements PaymentGateway CheckoutFacade.checkout() RetryingNotifier Lazy-loading repository
Also known as Anti-corruption layer (DDD, at scale) Application service Wrapper Surrogate

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

The red boundary is code you don't control. Everything to its left speaks PaymentStatus and BigDecimal; the adapters are the only classes that import vendor types. The facade sits above the port and orchestrates the subsystems, so a controller makes one call instead of five.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — two fictional vendor SDKs (AcmePay, ZetaPay) with deliberately different conventions, one adapter each, and a checkout facade.

// File: AdapterFacadeDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

// ================= Our port: designed for checkout's needs, not any vendor's =================
enum PaymentStatus { SUCCEEDED, PENDING, FAILED }

record PaymentResult(String providerRef, PaymentStatus status, String detail) {}

interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInr);
}

// ================= Vendor SDKs: pretend these are jars we cannot edit =================
final class AcmePayClient {
    /** Amount in paise; returns a loosely typed map with vendor status strings. */
    Map<String, String> createCharge(long amountPaise, String currency, String idempotencyKey) {
        String status = amountPaise > 500_000 ? "requires_action" : "succeeded";   // > ₹5,000 needs 3DS
        return Map.of("id", "ch_" + idempotencyKey, "status", status);
    }
}

final class ZetaPaySdk {
    static final class ZetaTimeoutException extends Exception {
        ZetaTimeoutException(String msg) { super(msg); }
    }

    record ZetaResponse(int code, String txnRef, String message) {}   // 0 ok, 1 pending, 5xx declined

    ZetaResponse pay(String merchantTxnId, String amountRupees) throws ZetaTimeoutException {
        if (merchantTxnId.endsWith("-slow")) throw new ZetaTimeoutException("read timed out after 10s");
        if (new BigDecimal(amountRupees).compareTo(new BigDecimal("10000")) > 0) {
            return new ZetaResponse(503, null, "LIMIT_EXCEEDED");
        }
        return new ZetaResponse(0, "ZP" + merchantTxnId.hashCode(), "OK");
    }
}

// ================= Adapters: the only classes that know vendor types =================
final class AcmePayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final AcmePayClient client;
    AcmePayAdapter(AcmePayClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInr) {
        long paise = amountInr.movePointRight(2).longValueExact();   // throws if fractional paise: never round money silently
        Map<String, String> raw = client.createCharge(paise, "INR", orderId);   // orderId doubles as idempotency key
        PaymentStatus status = switch (raw.get("status")) {
            case "succeeded" -> PaymentStatus.SUCCEEDED;
            case "requires_action", "processing" -> PaymentStatus.PENDING;
            default -> PaymentStatus.FAILED;
        };
        return new PaymentResult(raw.get("id"), status, "acme:" + raw.get("status"));
    }
}

final class ZetaPayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final ZetaPaySdk sdk;
    ZetaPayAdapter(ZetaPaySdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }

    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInr) {
        try {
            ZetaPaySdk.ZetaResponse r = sdk.pay(orderId, amountInr.toPlainString());
            PaymentStatus status = switch (r.code()) {
                case 0 -> PaymentStatus.SUCCEEDED;
                case 1 -> PaymentStatus.PENDING;
                default -> PaymentStatus.FAILED;
            };
            return new PaymentResult(r.txnRef(), status, "zeta:" + r.message());
        } catch (ZetaPaySdk.ZetaTimeoutException e) {
            // The request may have reached the provider: outcome UNKNOWN, not FAILED.
            return new PaymentResult(null, PaymentStatus.PENDING, "timeout, reconcile: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

// ================= Subsystems behind the facade =================
final class InventoryService {
    void hold(List<String> seats) { System.out.println("  inventory: hold " + seats); }
    void confirm(List<String> seats) { System.out.println("  inventory: confirm " + seats); }
    void release(List<String> seats) { System.out.println("  inventory: release " + seats); }
}

final class NotificationService {
    void send(String orderId, String text) { System.out.println("  notify " + orderId + ": " + text); }
}

// ================= Facade: one call for the controller =================
final class CheckoutFacade {
    private final InventoryService inventory;
    private final PaymentGateway payments;
    private final NotificationService notifications;

    CheckoutFacade(InventoryService inventory, PaymentGateway payments, NotificationService notifications) {
        this.inventory = inventory;
        this.payments = payments;
        this.notifications = notifications;
    }

    PaymentStatus checkout(String orderId, List<String> seats, BigDecimal amountInr) {
        inventory.hold(seats);
        PaymentResult result = payments.charge(orderId, amountInr);
        switch (result.status()) {
            case SUCCEEDED -> { inventory.confirm(seats); notifications.send(orderId, "booked " + seats); }
            case FAILED -> { inventory.release(seats); notifications.send(orderId, "payment failed"); }
            case PENDING -> System.out.println("  keep hold; reconcile later (" + result.detail() + ")");
        }
        return result.status();
    }
}

public class AdapterFacadeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        InventoryService inventory = new InventoryService();
        NotificationService notifications = new NotificationService();

        CheckoutFacade acme = new CheckoutFacade(inventory, new AcmePayAdapter(new AcmePayClient()), notifications);
        CheckoutFacade zeta = new CheckoutFacade(inventory, new ZetaPayAdapter(new ZetaPaySdk()), notifications);

        System.out.println("o-1 via Acme  -> " + acme.checkout("o-1", List.of("A7"), new BigDecimal("370.00")));
        System.out.println("o-2 via Zeta  -> " + zeta.checkout("o-2", List.of("B1", "B2"), new BigDecimal("12000.00")));
        System.out.println("o-3 via Zeta  -> " + zeta.checkout("o-3-slow", List.of("C4"), new BigDecimal("370.00")));
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same boundary. The vendor classes stand in for third-party packages.

# File: adapter_facade_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Protocol


# ================= Our port =================
class PaymentStatus(Enum):
    SUCCEEDED = "SUCCEEDED"
    PENDING = "PENDING"
    FAILED = "FAILED"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaymentResult:
    provider_ref: Optional[str]
    status: PaymentStatus
    detail: str


class PaymentGateway(Protocol):
    def charge(self, order_id: str, amount_inr: Decimal) -> PaymentResult: ...


# ================= Vendor SDKs (cannot edit) =================
class AcmePayClient:
    def create_charge(self, amount_paise: int, currency: str, idempotency_key: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
        status = "requires_action" if amount_paise > 500_000 else "succeeded"
        return {"id": f"ch_{idempotency_key}", "status": status}


class ZetaTimeout(Exception):
    pass


class ZetaPaySdk:
    def pay(self, merchant_txn_id: str, amount_rupees: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
        if merchant_txn_id.endswith("-slow"):
            raise ZetaTimeout("read timed out after 10s")
        if Decimal(amount_rupees) > Decimal("10000"):
            return {"code": 503, "txn_ref": None, "message": "LIMIT_EXCEEDED"}
        return {"code": 0, "txn_ref": f"ZP-{merchant_txn_id}", "message": "OK"}


# ================= Adapters =================
class AcmePayAdapter:
    _STATUS = {"succeeded": PaymentStatus.SUCCEEDED, "requires_action": PaymentStatus.PENDING,
               "processing": PaymentStatus.PENDING}

    def __init__(self, client: AcmePayClient) -> None:
        self._client = client

    def charge(self, order_id: str, amount_inr: Decimal) -> PaymentResult:
        paise = amount_inr * 100
        if paise != paise.to_integral_value():
            raise ValueError(f"fractional paise in {amount_inr}")      # never round money silently
        raw = self._client.create_charge(int(paise), "INR", order_id)
        status = self._STATUS.get(raw["status"], PaymentStatus.FAILED)
        return PaymentResult(raw["id"], status, f"acme:{raw['status']}")


class ZetaPayAdapter:
    _CODES = {0: PaymentStatus.SUCCEEDED, 1: PaymentStatus.PENDING}

    def __init__(self, sdk: ZetaPaySdk) -> None:
        self._sdk = sdk

    def charge(self, order_id: str, amount_inr: Decimal) -> PaymentResult:
        try:
            r = self._sdk.pay(order_id, str(amount_inr))
        except ZetaTimeout as exc:
            return PaymentResult(None, PaymentStatus.PENDING, f"timeout, reconcile: {exc}")
        status = self._CODES.get(int(r["code"]), PaymentStatus.FAILED)
        return PaymentResult(r["txn_ref"], status, f"zeta:{r['message']}")


# ================= Subsystems + Facade =================
class InventoryService:
    def hold(self, seats: List[str]) -> None:
        print(f"  inventory: hold {seats}")

    def confirm(self, seats: List[str]) -> None:
        print(f"  inventory: confirm {seats}")

    def release(self, seats: List[str]) -> None:
        print(f"  inventory: release {seats}")


class NotificationService:
    def send(self, order_id: str, text: str) -> None:
        print(f"  notify {order_id}: {text}")


class CheckoutFacade:
    def __init__(self, inventory: InventoryService, payments: PaymentGateway,
                 notifications: NotificationService) -> None:
        self._inventory, self._payments, self._notifications = inventory, payments, notifications

    def checkout(self, order_id: str, seats: List[str], amount_inr: Decimal) -> PaymentStatus:
        self._inventory.hold(seats)
        result = self._payments.charge(order_id, amount_inr)
        if result.status is PaymentStatus.SUCCEEDED:
            self._inventory.confirm(seats)
            self._notifications.send(order_id, f"booked {seats}")
        elif result.status is PaymentStatus.FAILED:
            self._inventory.release(seats)
            self._notifications.send(order_id, "payment failed")
        else:
            print(f"  keep hold; reconcile later ({result.detail})")
        return result.status


if __name__ == "__main__":
    inventory, notifications = InventoryService(), NotificationService()
    acme = CheckoutFacade(inventory, AcmePayAdapter(AcmePayClient()), notifications)
    zeta = CheckoutFacade(inventory, ZetaPayAdapter(ZetaPaySdk()), notifications)

    print("o-1 via Acme  ->", acme.checkout("o-1", ["A7"], Decimal("370.00")).value)
    print("o-2 via Zeta  ->", zeta.checkout("o-2", ["B1", "B2"], Decimal("12000.00")).value)
    print("o-3 via Zeta  ->", zeta.checkout("o-3-slow", ["C4"], Decimal("370.00")).value)

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 acme.checkout("o-1", [A7], 370.00)
⚙️ facade → inventory.hold([A7])
🔌 AcmePayAdapter → 370.00 → 37000 paise → createCharge → {id: ch_o-1, status: "succeeded"}
🔀 map "succeeded" → SUCCEEDED
✅ facade → inventory.confirm([A7]) → notify "booked [A7]"                 → SUCCEEDED

📥 zeta.checkout("o-2", [B1,B2], 12000.00)
🔌 ZetaPayAdapter → "12000.00" → {code: 503, message: LIMIT_EXCEEDED}
🔀 map 503 → FAILED
❌ facade → inventory.release([B1,B2]) → notify "payment failed"           → FAILED

📥 zeta.checkout("o-3-slow", [C4], 370.00)
🔌 ZetaPayAdapter → sdk throws ZetaTimeoutException
🔀 map timeout → PENDING ("timeout, reconcile: read timed out after 10s")
⚠️ facade → keeps the hold, no release, no notification                    → PENDING

The o-3 line is the one to say out loud. If the adapter had mapped the timeout to FAILED, the facade would release seat C4 — and if the charge had actually gone through at the provider, the customer would be charged for a seat someone else can now buy. PENDING plus a reconciliation job (query the provider by orderId) is the correct contract.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • Only one provider exists and none is planned. A thin adapter is still cheap insurance for testability, but a full abstraction layer with a factory and config is premature (→ item 26).

  • The vendor SDK already matches your domain interface closely. An adapter that forwards every call unchanged is noise.

  • A facade that becomes a god class. If CheckoutFacade starts containing pricing, fraud and seat-selection logic, it's no longer simplifying a subsystem — it is the subsystem. Keep facades thin orchestration.

  • You'd hide capabilities callers genuinely need. A facade over a payment SDK that drops partial refunds forces callers around it; offer the simple path and keep the detailed interface reachable.

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "An adapter just renames methods."

Reality: Renaming is the trivial part. The adapter owns semantic translation — units, status vocabularies, error models, timeouts, idempotency — and every one of those is a place where one provider's meaning differs from another's. A timeout mapped as failure is a money bug, not a naming bug.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • ../02-oo-design-principles/12-interface-segregation-for-extension-points.md — the port interface is designed from the consumer's needs.

  • ../05-modeling-craft/37-never-use-double-for-money.md — unit conversion at the boundary without rounding.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • ../04-concurrency-in-lld/32-idempotency-keys.md — the order id passed as idempotency key, and reconciliation of PENDING.

  • 15-factory-and-abstract-factory.md — choosing which adapter per merchant is a factory/registry decision.

notes.title: Repository & Unit of Work

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Repository — Martin Fowler, PoEAA: Repository

  • Unit of Work — Martin Fowler, PoEAA: Unit of Work

  • Bonus — Repository Design Pattern - GeeksforGeeks

Vault catalogue entry: catalogue/structural.md.

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Repository in one line? A collection-like interface for aggregates, in domain terms, hiding how they're stored.
Unit of Work in one line? Tracks the objects changed in one business operation and commits them together or not at all.
The in-interview implementation? Interface + ConcurrentHashMap/synchronized map impl; "in production, JDBC with a unique constraint."

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

A repository gives the domain a collection-like interface — find, findAvailable, saveAll — so business code never sees SQL or maps. In the interview it's backed by an in-memory map; in production it's a JDBC implementation, and nothing else changes. Unit of Work is the follow-up for multi-object operations: a group booking must book all four seats or none. The unit of work collects the changed seats and commits them in one step, with a version check so two users can't both book the same seat.

3. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What's the difference between a Repository and a DAO?

A DAO is organised around tables and persistence operations: SeatDao.insert, update, selectByShowId — its vocabulary is the database's. A Repository is organised around domain aggregates and reads like a collection: showSeats.findAvailable(showId), saveAll(seats) — its vocabulary is the domain's, and one repository method may use several DAOs or queries underneath.

In an LLD round the practical distinction is placement: the repository interface lives with the domain model (it's part of how the domain talks), and implementations live at the edge. That's what lets the in-memory version in the interview be swapped for SQL later without touching BookingService (→ item 5).

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Group booking of four seats: Unit of Work, or lock the seats in order?

Seen in the wild: the BookMyShow follow-up "what if a user selects four seats and one is taken mid-checkout?"

Really testing: whether you can name the atomicity boundary and choose between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency for it.

Pessimistic, lock ordering: acquire a lock per seat in a global order (sorted seat id), check all are available, write all, release. It's correct in one process and avoids deadlock (→ item 31), but holds locks for the whole operation and doesn't extend across processes.

Optimistic, Unit of Work: load the seats with their versions, apply the domain change in memory, and commit all changes in one step that verifies every version is unchanged — if any seat moved, nothing is written and the caller retries or reports "seat taken." No locks are held while the user is thinking, and it maps directly onto a database transaction with UPDATE … WHERE version = ? plus a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id). For seat booking, where conflicts are rare relative to reads, optimistic is usually the better default; switch to pessimistic when conflicts are frequent (a flash sale on ten seats), because retry storms waste more than lock waits do.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Repository DAO Unit of Work Active Record
Vocabulary Domain aggregates Tables / rows Business transaction Row = object
Who saves Service calls save Service calls DAO UoW commits tracked changes Object saves itself
Domain knows persistence? interface only often tightly coupled
Multi-object atomicity Per call Per call core purpose Manual
Real-world example Spring Data repositories JDBC DAO classes JPA EntityManager / Hibernate session Rails ActiveRecord

5. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Two rules make it atomic: validate every version before writing anything, and do validate-then-write inside one critical section (in memory) or one transaction (in a database). The version increments on each successful write, so a stale reader's commit is detected rather than silently overwriting.

7. Code Example — Java then Python

Java 17 — a ShowSeat aggregate with a version, a repository interface with an in-memory implementation, and a unit of work for group booking. The race between two users is interleaved by hand so the conflict is deterministic.

// File: RepositoryDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

enum SeatState { AVAILABLE, BOOKED }

final class SeatUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {
    SeatUnavailableException(String key) { super("seat " + key + " is not available"); }
}

final class ConcurrencyConflictException extends RuntimeException {
    ConcurrencyConflictException(String key) { super("seat " + key + " changed since it was loaded"); }
}

// Aggregate: status lives on ShowSeat (per show), never on Seat.
record ShowSeat(String showId, String seatId, SeatState state, String bookingId, long version) {
    String key() { return showId + ":" + seatId; }

    ShowSeat book(String newBookingId) {                 // domain rule lives on the aggregate
        if (state != SeatState.AVAILABLE) throw new SeatUnavailableException(key());
        return new ShowSeat(showId, seatId, SeatState.BOOKED, newBookingId, version);
    }
}

// ---------- Repository: domain vocabulary, no storage details ----------
interface ShowSeatRepository {
    Optional<ShowSeat> find(String showId, String seatId);
    List<ShowSeat> findAvailable(String showId);
    /** All-or-nothing; each seat's version must match what's stored. */
    void saveAll(List<ShowSeat> changed);
}

final class InMemoryShowSeatRepository implements ShowSeatRepository {
    private final Map<String, ShowSeat> rows = new HashMap<>();   // guarded by "this"

    synchronized void seed(ShowSeat seat) { rows.put(seat.key(), seat); }

    @Override
    public synchronized Optional<ShowSeat> find(String showId, String seatId) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(rows.get(showId + ":" + seatId));
    }

    @Override
    public synchronized List<ShowSeat> findAvailable(String showId) {
        List<ShowSeat> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ShowSeat s : rows.values()) {
            if (s.showId().equals(showId) && s.state() == SeatState.AVAILABLE) out.add(s);
        }
        out.sort((a, b) -> a.seatId().compareTo(b.seatId()));
        return out;
    }

    @Override
    public synchronized void saveAll(List<ShowSeat> changed) {
        for (ShowSeat c : changed) {                                  // 1. validate everything first
            ShowSeat current = rows.get(c.key());
            if (current == null || current.version() != c.version()) throw new ConcurrencyConflictException(c.key());
        }
        for (ShowSeat c : changed) {                                  // 2. then write everything
            rows.put(c.key(), new ShowSeat(c.showId(), c.seatId(), c.state(), c.bookingId(), c.version() + 1));
        }
    }
    // Production: a JdbcShowSeatRepository doing this in one transaction with
    // UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?  plus UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id). Nothing above it changes.
}

// ---------- Unit of Work: one business operation, one commit ----------
final class UnitOfWork {
    private final ShowSeatRepository repository;
    private final Map<String, ShowSeat> dirty = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    UnitOfWork(ShowSeatRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }

    ShowSeat load(String showId, String seatId) {
        return repository.find(showId, seatId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no seat " + showId + ":" + seatId));
    }

    void registerDirty(ShowSeat seat) { dirty.put(seat.key(), seat); }

    void commit() {
        repository.saveAll(List.copyOf(dirty.values()));
        dirty.clear();
    }
}

final class BookingService {
    private final ShowSeatRepository repository;
    BookingService(ShowSeatRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }

    void bookGroup(String showId, List<String> seatIds, String bookingId) {
        UnitOfWork uow = new UnitOfWork(repository);
        for (String seatId : seatIds) {
            uow.registerDirty(uow.load(showId, seatId).book(bookingId));   // throws before commit if unavailable
        }
        uow.commit();
    }
}

public class RepositoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        InMemoryShowSeatRepository repo = new InMemoryShowSeatRepository();
        for (String id : List.of("A1", "A2", "A3", "A4")) {
            repo.seed(new ShowSeat("show-42", id, SeatState.AVAILABLE, null, 0));
        }
        BookingService bookings = new BookingService(repo);

        bookings.bookGroup("show-42", List.of("A1", "A2"), "bk-alice");
        System.out.println("alice booked A1,A2; available = " + ids(repo.findAvailable("show-42")));

        try {
            bookings.bookGroup("show-42", List.of("A2", "A3"), "bk-bob");
        } catch (SeatUnavailableException e) {
            System.out.println("bob rejected: " + e.getMessage() + "; available = " + ids(repo.findAvailable("show-42")));
        }

        // carol and dave both load A3, A4 at version 0 before either commits.
        UnitOfWork carol = new UnitOfWork(repo);
        UnitOfWork dave = new UnitOfWork(repo);
        for (String id : List.of("A3", "A4")) {
            carol.registerDirty(carol.load("show-42", id).book("bk-carol"));
            dave.registerDirty(dave.load("show-42", id).book("bk-dave"));
        }
        carol.commit();
        try {
            dave.commit();
        } catch (ConcurrencyConflictException e) {
            System.out.println("dave conflict: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("A3 = " + repo.find("show-42", "A3").orElseThrow());
        System.out.println("A4 = " + repo.find("show-42", "A4").orElseThrow());
    }

    private static List<String> ids(List<ShowSeat> seats) {
        return seats.stream().map(ShowSeat::seatId).toList();
    }
}

Python 3.9+ — same design with typing.Protocol for the repository port.

# File: repository_demo.py
from __future__ import annotations

import dataclasses
import threading
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Protocol


class SeatState(Enum):
    AVAILABLE = "AVAILABLE"
    BOOKED = "BOOKED"


class SeatUnavailableError(Exception):
    pass


class ConcurrencyConflictError(Exception):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ShowSeat:
    show_id: str
    seat_id: str
    state: SeatState
    booking_id: Optional[str]
    version: int

    @property
    def key(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.show_id}:{self.seat_id}"

    def book(self, booking_id: str) -> "ShowSeat":
        if self.state is not SeatState.AVAILABLE:
            raise SeatUnavailableError(f"seat {self.key} is not available")
        return dataclasses.replace(self, state=SeatState.BOOKED, booking_id=booking_id)


class ShowSeatRepository(Protocol):
    def find(self, show_id: str, seat_id: str) -> Optional[ShowSeat]: ...
    def find_available(self, show_id: str) -> List[ShowSeat]: ...
    def save_all(self, changed: List[ShowSeat]) -> None: ...


class InMemoryShowSeatRepository:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._rows: Dict[str, ShowSeat] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def seed(self, seat: ShowSeat) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._rows[seat.key] = seat

    def find(self, show_id: str, seat_id: str) -> Optional[ShowSeat]:
        with self._lock:
            return self._rows.get(f"{show_id}:{seat_id}")

    def find_available(self, show_id: str) -> List[ShowSeat]:
        with self._lock:
            return sorted((s for s in self._rows.values()
                           if s.show_id == show_id and s.state is SeatState.AVAILABLE),
                          key=lambda s: s.seat_id)

    def save_all(self, changed: List[ShowSeat]) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            for c in changed:                                   # validate all
                current = self._rows.get(c.key)
                if current is None or current.version != c.version:
                    raise ConcurrencyConflictError(f"seat {c.key} changed since it was loaded")
            for c in changed:                                   # then write all
                self._rows[c.key] = dataclasses.replace(c, version=c.version + 1)


class UnitOfWork:
    def __init__(self, repository: ShowSeatRepository) -> None:
        self._repository = repository
        self._dirty: Dict[str, ShowSeat] = {}

    def load(self, show_id: str, seat_id: str) -> ShowSeat:
        seat = self._repository.find(show_id, seat_id)
        if seat is None:
            raise KeyError(f"no seat {show_id}:{seat_id}")
        return seat

    def register_dirty(self, seat: ShowSeat) -> None:
        self._dirty[seat.key] = seat

    def commit(self) -> None:
        self._repository.save_all(list(self._dirty.values()))
        self._dirty.clear()


class BookingService:
    def __init__(self, repository: ShowSeatRepository) -> None:
        self._repository = repository

    def book_group(self, show_id: str, seat_ids: List[str], booking_id: str) -> None:
        uow = UnitOfWork(self._repository)
        for seat_id in seat_ids:
            uow.register_dirty(uow.load(show_id, seat_id).book(booking_id))
        uow.commit()


def ids(seats: List[ShowSeat]) -> List[str]:
    return [s.seat_id for s in seats]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    repo = InMemoryShowSeatRepository()
    for sid in ["A1", "A2", "A3", "A4"]:
        repo.seed(ShowSeat("show-42", sid, SeatState.AVAILABLE, None, 0))
    bookings = BookingService(repo)

    bookings.book_group("show-42", ["A1", "A2"], "bk-alice")
    print("alice booked A1,A2; available =", ids(repo.find_available("show-42")))

    try:
        bookings.book_group("show-42", ["A2", "A3"], "bk-bob")
    except SeatUnavailableError as e:
        print(f"bob rejected: {e}; available =", ids(repo.find_available("show-42")))

    carol, dave = UnitOfWork(repo), UnitOfWork(repo)
    for sid in ["A3", "A4"]:
        carol.register_dirty(carol.load("show-42", sid).book("bk-carol"))
        dave.register_dirty(dave.load("show-42", sid).book("bk-dave"))
    carol.commit()
    try:
        dave.commit()
    except ConcurrencyConflictError as e:
        print("dave conflict:", e)
    print("A3 =", repo.find("show-42", "A3"))
    print("A4 =", repo.find("show-42", "A4"))

8. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

📥 seed show-42: A1..A4 AVAILABLE v0

⚙️ alice bookGroup [A1,A2]
   load A1 v0 → book → dirty · load A2 v0 → book → dirty
   commit → validate A1 v0 ✅ A2 v0 ✅ → write A1,A2 BOOKED v1
🎯 available = [A3, A4]

⚙️ bob bookGroup [A2,A3]
   load A2 v1 BOOKED → book() ❌ SeatUnavailableException   (before commit — A3 never registered)
🎯 available = [A3, A4]   nothing changed

🧵 carol and dave each load A3 v0, A4 v0 and register BOOKED
⚙️ carol.commit → validate A3 v0 ✅ A4 v0 ✅ → write both, now v1 (bk-carol)
❌ dave.commit  → validate A3: stored v1 ≠ loaded v0 → ConcurrencyConflictException
                  A4 check never reached; no write happened for either seat
🎯 A3 = BOOKED bk-carol v1 · A4 = BOOKED bk-carol v1

Two different failures, two different layers. Bob's rejection is a domain rule caught on the aggregate before any commit. Dave's is a concurrency conflict caught at commit by the version check — his in-memory view was correct when he loaded it, and wrong by the time he wrote. Both leave the store unchanged, which is the all-or-nothing guarantee.

10. When NOT To Use This

  • A small CRUD service with no domain logic. A repository layer over a table the service just reads and writes adds indirection without isolating anything; Spring Data or a thin DAO is enough.

  • Unit of Work on single-object operations. One save is already atomic; tracking dirty sets for it is ceremony.

  • Hand-rolling Unit of Work on top of an ORM that already provides one. JPA's persistence context and Hibernate's session are units of work; a second one on top creates two sources of truth about what's dirty.

  • Hiding queries the domain genuinely needs to shape. A generic Repository<T> with only findById/save pushes filtering into services and loads whole tables; repository methods should be named domain queries (findAvailable(showId)).

11. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "The repository interface should return whatever the database returns — rows, nullable fields, IDs."

Reality: The interface belongs to the domain and returns domain aggregates in valid states (ShowSeat with a real SeatState, Optional for absence). Persistence details — rows, nullable columns, SQL exceptions — are translated inside the implementation, the same way an adapter translates a vendor SDK (→ item 24).

Pointer note. The full treatment lives in the vault's pattern catalogue: catalogue/anti-patterns.md. This file carries only what the LLD round needs: when to reach for it, and the follow-up it absorbs.

In one line

Applying six patterns to a parking lot is a negative signal.

In the round

The rule: name a pattern only when it removes a specific future edit you can articulate.

The budget: three or four extension points in a 60-minute round, placed on the axes the problem statement hints at. Spending them uniformly is overuse; spending none is the mid-level design.

What overuse looks like: an interface with one implementation and no named future requirement; a factory for a class with one constructor; a State machine for three states and two transitions; a Builder for a three-field record.

The stronger sentence is always the specific one. "I'll use Strategy here" scores less than "pricing will change, so it goes behind an interface and weekend pricing becomes a new class rather than an if" — same design, roughly twice the credit.
